title: Scheduled Self Forcing: Curriculum-Based Exposure Blending for Robust Autoregressive Video Diffusion
description:
Problem: Self Forcing fully conditions on self-generated frames during training, which can destabilize early training when the model produces very noisy outputs, leading to compounding errors that slow convergence. Meanwhile, purely teacher-forced models suffer from exposure bias at inference. A principled interpolation between these extremes during training remains unexplored for video diffusion.

Proposed Method: We introduce Scheduled Self Forcing (SSF), a curriculum training strategy that gradually transitions the KV cache context from ground-truth frames toward self-generated frames as training progresses. Specifically, we define a blending schedule α(t) ∈ [0,1] that mixes ground-truth and self-generated KV cache entries at each training step. Early training uses predominantly ground-truth context (α≈0) for stability, while late training approaches full self-forcing (α→1) to eliminate exposure bias. We further propose per-frame stochastic blending, where each cached frame is independently drawn from ground-truth or self-generated distribution with probability α(t), creating diverse training contexts that improve robustness.

Experiments: (1) Compare convergence speed and final FVD/FID on UCF-101, Kinetics-600, and an open-domain streaming benchmark against vanilla Self Forcing and teacher forcing baselines. (2) Ablate schedule shapes (linear, cosine, step) and stochastic vs. deterministic blending. (3) Evaluate long-horizon generation stability via 60-second extrapolation tests measuring temporal consistency degradation. (4) Analyze sensitivity to model capacity and noise levels in early training.

title: Temporal Consistency Rewards: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback for Autoregressive Video Diffusion
description:
Problem: While Self Forcing addresses exposure bias through autoregressive rollout training, the holistic video-level loss still relies on pixel-level reconstruction objectives that poorly capture perceptual quality dimensions humans care about—temporal coherence, motion naturalness, and semantic consistency across long sequences. Standard diffusion losses cannot easily encode these high-level preferences.

Proposed Method: We introduce RLHF-Video, which augments the Self Forcing training paradigm with reinforcement learning from human feedback. During Self Forcing's autoregressive rollout, instead of (or in addition to) the diffusion loss, we compute rewards from: (1) a learned temporal consistency reward model trained on human preference annotations comparing video clips on smoothness and coherence, (2) a pretrained video-text alignment scorer (e.g., VideoCLIP) for semantic fidelity, and (3) a motion naturalness discriminator. We apply these rewards via a sequence-level policy gradient, using the KV-cache rollout graph from Self Forcing as the computational backbone. Stochastic gradient truncation from Self Forcing naturally regularizes the RL optimization.

Experiments: We collect ~50K human preference pairs on temporal coherence and motion quality. We compare against Self Forcing baseline, DDPO-style approaches, and non-causal models on UCF-101, WebVid, and a new long-video benchmark (>30s) measuring temporal drift, FVD, and human preference win-rates. We ablate reward combinations and RL algorithms (PPO vs. REINFORCE).

title: Curriculum Self Forcing: Progressive Rollout Horizon Scheduling for Stable Long-Video Autoregressive Diffusion Training
description:
Problem: Self Forcing's training-time autoregressive rollout, while bridging the train-test gap, introduces compounding error accumulation that destabilizes training when the rollout horizon is long. Early in training, the model generates highly noisy frames that corrupt subsequent generation steps, leading to gradient explosions and slow convergence for video sequences exceeding ~30 seconds.

Proposed Method: We introduce Curriculum Self Forcing, which schedules the autoregressive rollout horizon as a curriculum during training. Initially, the model trains with short rollout windows (2-4 frames) nearly identical to standard teacher forcing, then progressively extends the horizon as the model stabilizes. We combine this with an adaptive stochastic truncation strategy that dynamically adjusts truncation probability based on per-step gradient norm variance. Additionally, we introduce a 'rollout quality gating' mechanism that skips gradient updates through temporally corrupted frames (detected via perceptual quality thresholds), preventing degenerate self-generated context from poisoning future frame supervision.

Experiments: (1) Compare convergence stability and final quality against vanilla Self Forcing on UCF-101, Kinetics-600, and OpenDV-YouTube across horizons of 64/128/256 frames. (2) Ablate curriculum schedules (linear, cosine, step-wise). (3) Measure FVD and temporal consistency at 1-5 minute generation lengths. (4) Evaluate computational overhead of quality gating relative to generation quality gains.

title: Adaptive KV Cache Compression for Long-Horizon Autoregressive Video Diffusion via Temporal Saliency Pruning
description: Problem: Self Forcing's rolling KV cache mechanism enables streaming video generation but faces a fundamental memory-quality tradeoff: retaining too few past frames loses long-range temporal coherence (scene consistency, object permanence), while retaining too many makes generation prohibitively slow and memory-intensive for truly long videos (minutes-scale). Current rolling cache uses a fixed window, agnostic to semantic content. Proposed Method: We introduce Temporal Saliency-Guided KV Cache Compression (TSKC), which dynamically selects which past frame representations to retain in the KV cache based on learned temporal saliency scores. A lightweight attention-based saliency predictor, trained jointly with the diffusion model, assigns importance weights to cached frames by measuring their cross-attention contribution to current frame generation. Frames below an adaptive threshold are compressed into compact 'summary tokens' via a learned pooling operation rather than fully discarded. This creates a hierarchical cache: recent frames at full resolution, older frames as compressed summaries. The saliency predictor is trained with a consistency regularization loss that penalizes semantic drift over long sequences. Experiments: We evaluate on long-form video benchmarks (VBench-Long, custom minute-scale generation), measuring temporal consistency (CLIP similarity over 200+ frames), memory usage, and generation speed, comparing against fixed-window rolling cache and full-cache baselines.

title: Reward-Guided Self Forcing: Aligning Autoregressive Video Diffusion with Human Preferences via Online RLHF
description:
Problem: While Self Forcing addresses exposure bias in autoregressive video diffusion, the holistic video-level loss still relies on reconstruction objectives that may not align with human perceptual preferences (e.g., aesthetic quality, motion naturalness, temporal coherence). Existing RLHF approaches for video generation require full sequence rollouts disconnected from training, making them prohibitively expensive.

Proposed Method: We extend Self Forcing's autoregressive rollout mechanism to enable online reinforcement learning from human feedback. Since Self Forcing already performs full video rollouts during training with KV caching, we augment the training loop with a lightweight video reward model (trained on human preference annotations) that scores complete generated sequences. Using the stochastic gradient truncation strategy from Self Forcing, we backpropagate reward signals through truncated rollout windows, combining reconstruction loss with a PPO-style policy gradient objective. The rolling KV cache enables efficient credit assignment across temporal segments without storing full computation graphs.

Experiments: (1) Train reward model on VideoFeedback/EvalCrafter human preference datasets; (2) Compare against reconstruction-only Self Forcing on aesthetic scores, motion quality metrics, and human evaluation studies; (3) Ablate reward signal window sizes and truncation strategies; (4) Evaluate on text-to-video benchmarks (VBench, EvalCrafter) demonstrating improved alignment without sacrificing generation speed or temporal consistency.

title: Curriculum Self Forcing: Adaptive Exposure Scheduling for Long-Horizon Video Generation
description: Problem: Self Forcing eliminates exposure bias by training exclusively on self-generated context, but this cold-start approach forces the model to immediately handle its own worst-quality outputs from the very beginning of training, potentially destabilizing early optimization and limiting convergence quality for very long sequences (>1000 frames). Proposed Method: We introduce Curriculum Self Forcing, which dynamically interpolates between ground-truth conditioning and fully self-generated conditioning throughout training via a learned exposure schedule. Concretely, at each training step, a per-frame mixing probability p(t, frame_idx) determines whether each KV-cache entry comes from ground truth or the model's own generation. This probability starts near 1.0 (ground truth) and decays according to a learned curriculum controller that monitors a sequence-level quality signal (FVD on held-out clips). The controller uses a bandit-style update rule to accelerate or decelerate curriculum progression, ensuring the model is always challenged but not overwhelmed. For very long sequences, we additionally introduce a spatial curriculum where earlier frames receive ground-truth context longer than later frames. Experiments: (1) Ablation against fixed schedules and pure Self Forcing on UCF-101, Kinetics-600, and WebVid; (2) Long-horizon extrapolation benchmarks (>2 minutes at 24fps); (3) Training stability analysis (gradient variance, FVD vs. training steps); (4) Downstream task: video prediction with sparse conditioning frames.

title: Reward-Guided Self Forcing: Aligning Autoregressive Video Diffusion with Human Preferences via Holistic Trajectory Optimization
description:
Problem: Self Forcing enables efficient autoregressive video generation by closing the train-test gap, but the holistic video-level loss still relies on pixel reconstruction objectives that poorly correlate with human aesthetic preferences, temporal coherence, and semantic faithfulness to text prompts. This leaves a gap between technically coherent videos and genuinely preferred outputs.

Proposed Method: We extend Self Forcing's training paradigm by replacing or augmenting the holistic video-level loss with differentiable reward signals from pretrained video quality models (e.g., VideoScore, CLIP-based semantic alignment, motion smoothness estimators). During autoregressive rollout with KV caching, we backpropagate through the entire generated trajectory using reward-weighted policy gradient estimates combined with stochastic gradient truncation inherited from Self Forcing. We introduce a multi-objective reward aggregation scheme that balances aesthetic quality, prompt adherence, and temporal consistency without mode collapse, using a learned reward baseline to reduce variance.

Experiments: (1) Compare against vanilla Self Forcing and RLHF-finetuned non-causal models on EvalCrafter and T2V-CompBench; (2) Ablate individual reward components and truncation horizons; (3) Human preference studies comparing reward-aligned vs. reconstruction-only Self Forcing; (4) Measure inference latency to confirm real-time generation is preserved post-alignment.

title: Adaptive KV Cache Compression for Long-Horizon Autoregressive Video Diffusion via Temporal Saliency Gating
description:
Problem: Self Forcing's rolling KV cache enables streaming video generation but treats all cached frames uniformly, causing memory bottlenecks and quality degradation in very long-horizon generation (minutes-scale video) where temporally distant frames contribute unevenly to future frame generation. A principled mechanism for selectively retaining salient temporal context is needed.

Proposed Method: We introduce Temporal Saliency Gating (TSG), a learned compression module that dynamically scores and prunes KV cache entries based on their predicted relevance to future generation. TSG uses a lightweight attention-based scorer trained jointly with the diffusion model under Self Forcing's rollout paradigm, incorporating a sparsity regularization loss that encourages aggressive compression while penalizing quality degradation. We additionally propose a hierarchical cache structure retaining dense recent frames and sparsely sampled semantic keyframes from distant history, with compression ratios adapted to available GPU memory.

Experiments: (1) Long-horizon video generation benchmarks (500+ frames) comparing memory usage, FVD, and temporal consistency against fixed rolling window baselines; (2) Ablations on compression ratio schedules and scorer architectures; (3) Streaming latency profiling at different sequence lengths on single GPU; (4) Qualitative evaluation of scene coherence over extended temporal horizons on open-domain video datasets (WebVid, OpenVid-1M).

title: Contrastive Self Forcing: Leveraging Negative Rollouts for Temporal Consistency in Autoregressive Video Diffusion
description:
Problem: While Self Forcing addresses exposure bias through autoregressive rollout during training, the holistic video-level loss lacks explicit mechanisms to penalize specific failure modes like temporal flickering, object inconsistency, and motion artifacts that emerge over long rollout horizons. The model learns what good sequences look like but not actively what bad sequences look like.

Proposed Method: We introduce Contrastive Self Forcing (CSF), which augments the Self Forcing training paradigm with contrastive learning over multiple concurrent rollouts. During each training iteration, we generate K parallel rollouts using different noise seeds from the same conditioning frame, creating a diverse pool of candidate continuations. We then apply lightweight temporal consistency metrics (optical flow consistency, LPIPS between adjacent frames, CLIP-based semantic drift) to automatically rank rollouts as positive/negative pairs without human annotation. A contrastive objective (InfoNCE-style) is applied over the KV-cache representations, encouraging the model's internal state to cluster around temporally coherent generation trajectories. We additionally propose 'rollout surgery' — selectively swapping KV-cache segments between good and degraded rollouts to identify and penalize specific cache states responsible for quality collapse.

Experiments: (1) Long-horizon generation quality (100+ frames) vs. Self Forcing baseline; (2) Ablation of ranking metrics and number of parallel rollouts K; (3) Temporal consistency metrics (warping error, FVD) on UCF-101, Kinetics, and WebVid; (4) Computational overhead analysis vs. quality tradeoff.

title: Reward-Guided Self Forcing: Aligning Autoregressive Video Diffusion with Human Preferences via Sequence-Level RLHF
description: Problem: Current autoregressive video diffusion models, including Self Forcing, optimize frame reconstruction quality but lack alignment with human aesthetic preferences, semantic coherence, or task-specific rewards (e.g., physics plausibility, instruction following). The holistic sequence-level loss in Self Forcing creates a natural foundation for integrating external reward signals, which frame-wise objectives cannot easily accommodate. Proposed Method: We extend Self Forcing's training paradigm with a sequence-level reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) framework. During autoregressive rollout with KV caching, we generate complete video sequences and score them with a pretrained video reward model (covering aesthetic quality, motion smoothness, text-video alignment, and physical plausibility). We combine this reward signal with the diffusion denoising loss using a KL-regularized policy gradient objective, similar to RAFT/DPPO but adapted for streaming video generation. Stochastic gradient truncation from Self Forcing keeps backpropagation tractable across long sequences. A lightweight reward model trained on human preference annotations over generated video clips provides dense sequence-level feedback. Experiments: (1) Text-to-video generation evaluated on human preference studies vs. RLHF-free baselines; (2) Instruction-following metrics on EvalCrafter and T2V-CompBench; (3) Ablations on reward model design and KL regularization strength; (4) Analysis of reward hacking and temporal consistency under extended generation.

title: Adaptive KV Cache Compression for Long-Horizon Autoregressive Video Diffusion via Importance-Weighted Token Pruning
description:
Problem: Self Forcing's rolling KV cache enables streaming video generation but treats all cached context tokens equally, causing memory overhead to scale linearly with sequence length and limiting coherent long-horizon generation (e.g., minutes-long videos). As temporal distance grows, early context contributes unevenly—some tokens anchor global scene structure while others are transient details—yet no mechanism exists to selectively retain high-value temporal context.

Proposed Method: We introduce Adaptive Temporal Cache Compression (ATCC), which learns to dynamically prune and compress the KV cache based on cross-frame attention importance scores computed during the Self Forcing training rollout. Specifically, we train a lightweight importance predictor (a small MLP head on attention weights) that scores each cached token's relevance to future frame generation. Low-importance tokens are merged via learned pooling into compact summary tokens, while high-importance tokens are retained verbatim. The importance predictor is trained end-to-end alongside the diffusion model using the same holistic video-level loss from Self Forcing, enabling gradient signals from future frames to teach the model which past context matters most.

Experiments: (1) Long-video generation quality at 500+ frames vs. fixed rolling window baselines; (2) Memory-quality Pareto curves at varying compression ratios; (3) Scene consistency metrics (CLIP similarity, FID) for multi-minute generation; (4) Ablations comparing learned vs. heuristic pruning strategies on UCF-101 and WebVid.

title: Reward-Guided Self Forcing: Aligning Autoregressive Video Diffusion with Temporal Coherence via Online RLHF
description: Problem: Self Forcing bridges the train-test gap via autoregressive rollout, but the holistic video-level loss still relies on reconstruction objectives that poorly capture perceptual quality dimensions like temporal coherence, motion naturalness, and semantic consistency across long sequences. Human preferences about video quality are notoriously misaligned with pixel-level losses. Proposed Method: We propose Reward-Guided Self Forcing, which replaces or augments the holistic video-level loss with learned reward signals during the autoregressive rollout. Specifically, we train lightweight reward models on human preference annotations for temporal coherence and motion quality, then integrate these rewards into the Self Forcing training loop via a REINFORCE-style policy gradient applied through the stochastic gradient truncation mechanism already present in Self Forcing. We additionally introduce a 'coherence critic' that scores KV cache context quality, penalizing accumulated drift in cached representations. Experiments: (1) We evaluate on standard benchmarks (UCF-101, Kinetics, EvalCrafter) comparing FVD, temporal consistency metrics, and human preference scores against vanilla Self Forcing and non-causal baselines. (2) We ablate reward model architectures and gradient truncation lengths. (3) We test long-video extrapolation (500+ frames) to measure drift reduction. (4) We assess real-time latency preservation on a single GPU.

title: Adaptive KV Cache Compression for Long-Horizon Autoregressive Video Diffusion via Temporal Saliency Routing
description:
Problem: Self Forcing's rolling KV cache enables efficient video extrapolation, but naively retaining fixed-size context windows discards potentially critical long-range temporal information (scene identity, character consistency, physics coherence) while wasting capacity on redundant nearby frames. For very long videos (minutes-scale), this leads to semantic drift despite eliminating exposure bias.

Proposed Method: We introduce Temporal Saliency Routing (TSR), a learned mechanism that dynamically allocates KV cache slots across a hierarchical temporal memory. Rather than a uniform rolling window, TSR maintains three cache tiers: (1) a dense recent window (last N frames), (2) a sparse 'landmark' cache storing high-saliency keyframes selected via a lightweight learned importance scorer trained with gradient signals from the holistic video-level loss, and (3) a compressed episodic summary embedding updated via an EMA-based memory distillation module. During denoising, cross-attention queries route to all three tiers with learned mixing weights.

Experiments: (1) Long-video generation benchmarks (EvalCrafter, VideoPhy) measuring semantic consistency over 500+ frames; (2) Ablations comparing uniform rolling cache vs. TSR tiers; (3) Human evaluation on character/scene identity preservation; (4) Memory-quality Pareto curves vs. baselines; (5) Streaming latency on single GPU to verify real-time capability is maintained.

title: Curriculum Self Forcing: Adaptive Exposure Scheduling for Long-Horizon Video Generation
description: Problem: Self Forcing eliminates exposure bias by always conditioning on self-generated frames during training, but this abrupt switch from teacher-forcing to full self-forcing can cause training instability and slow convergence, especially for long video sequences where early errors compound aggressively. A curriculum that gradually transitions between ground-truth and self-generated conditioning could improve both stability and final quality. Proposed Method: We introduce Curriculum Self Forcing, which replaces the binary ground-truth/self-generated conditioning with a scheduled mixture policy. At each training step, conditioning frames are sampled from a mixture distribution parameterized by a curriculum schedule β(t): with probability β(t), use ground-truth frames; with probability 1-β(t), use self-generated frames. β(t) is annealed from 1.0 to 0.0 following an adaptive schedule informed by a proxy signal—specifically, the temporal FVD computed on a held-out validation set. We additionally explore frame-position-dependent scheduling, where closer frames use more ground-truth context while distant frames use self-generated context, reflecting the natural difficulty gradient in autoregressive generation. Experiments: We evaluate on UCF-101, WebVid, and a long-horizon driving dataset (nuPlan), measuring FVD, temporal consistency, and training wall-clock time versus Self Forcing and teacher-forcing baselines across 16, 64, and 256 frame horizons.

title: Hierarchical Self Forcing: Bridging Semantic and Temporal Consistency in Long-Form Video Generation via Multi-Scale Autoregressive Rollout
description: Problem: Self Forcing addresses frame-level exposure bias but struggles with long-range semantic drift in extended videos (>1 minute), where locally coherent frames gradually lose global narrative consistency—characters change appearance, scenes shift implausibly, and storylines diverge. A single rolling KV cache captures low-level temporal context but cannot maintain high-level semantic intent across hundreds of frames. Proposed Method: We introduce Hierarchical Self Forcing, which augments the autoregressive rollout with a two-level cache structure: (1) a dense short-term KV cache (existing mechanism) for fine-grained temporal coherence, and (2) a sparse semantic summary cache that periodically compresses past generated segments into compact latent summaries via a learned temporal attention pooling module. During training rollout, both caches condition future generation, and the holistic loss is extended to include a semantic consistency term measured via CLIP-space trajectory smoothness over the full rollout. Stochastic gradient truncation is applied asymmetrically—shorter windows for the dense cache, longer windows for the semantic cache to propagate global gradients. Experiments: We evaluate on long-form video benchmarks (VBench-Long, EvalCrafter extended splits), measuring semantic consistency via CLIP drift metrics, FVD at 30s/60s/120s horizons, and character identity preservation scores. Ablations isolate contributions of each cache level and the semantic consistency loss.

title: Reward-Guided Self Forcing: Aligning Autoregressive Video Diffusion with Human Preferences via Online Rollout Optimization
description: Problem: Self Forcing bridges the train-test gap but still optimizes surrogate pixel-level losses that poorly correlate with human preference metrics like aesthetic quality, motion smoothness, or semantic faithfulness. Integrating reward models into autoregressive video diffusion training is non-trivial because reward signals are typically non-differentiable and evaluated over full sequences. Proposed Method: We extend Self Forcing's autoregressive rollout framework to incorporate reward-based optimization. During training, we generate complete video rollouts using the rolling KV cache mechanism, then compute scalar rewards from pretrained video quality models (e.g., VideoScore, aesthetic predictors, optical flow smoothness estimators). We apply REINFORCE-style policy gradient updates alongside the standard diffusion loss, using stochastic gradient truncation to keep computational cost manageable. A reward-weighted importance sampling scheme stabilizes training by down-weighting low-reward trajectories. We also introduce a multi-reward Pareto optimization strategy to simultaneously optimize competing objectives without collapsing to single-reward modes. Experiments: We evaluate on (1) UCF-101 and WebVid benchmarks measuring FVD and human preference win rates, (2) long-video extrapolation coherence, (3) ablations on reward weighting, truncation depth, and multi-reward trade-offs, comparing against Self Forcing baseline and offline RLHF video diffusion approaches.

title: Reward-Guided Self Forcing: Aligning Autoregressive Video Diffusion with Human Preferences via Online RLHF
description: Problem: Self Forcing enables efficient autoregressive video generation by training on self-generated context, but the resulting videos, while temporally consistent, may still diverge from human aesthetic preferences (motion naturalness, semantic fidelity, visual quality) since training relies purely on pixel-level reconstruction objectives. Bridging the gap between perceptual quality and diffusion loss remains an open challenge. Proposed Method: We extend the Self Forcing framework with an online reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) loop. During training rollouts, we sample complete video clips using the rolling KV cache mechanism, then score them with a frozen video reward model (e.g., a fine-tuned VideoScore or aesthetics critic). We backpropagate reward signals through the truncated gradient graph already established by Self Forcing's stochastic truncation strategy, treating reward as an additional sequence-level objective alongside the holistic diffusion loss. To avoid reward hacking, we add a KL penalty against a reference policy checkpoint. Planned Experiments: (1) Compare reward-guided vs. baseline Self Forcing on EvalCrafter, VBench, and human preference studies. (2) Ablate reward model choices and KL penalty strength. (3) Measure training stability, latency overhead, and whether temporal coherence is preserved. (4) Test generalization to domain-specific rewards (e.g., physics plausibility for robotics video prediction).

title: Curriculum Self Forcing: Progressive Rollout Horizon Scheduling for Stable Long-Video Autoregressive Diffusion
description: Problem: Self Forcing trains autoregressive video diffusion models by conditioning on self-generated context from the very beginning of training. However, early in training when the model generates poor-quality frames, conditioning on these severely corrupted outputs creates an extremely difficult optimization landscape, potentially causing training instability or slow convergence for very long video sequences (hundreds of frames). The exposure to compounding errors may be too abrupt. Proposed Method: We introduce Curriculum Self Forcing, which gradually increases the autoregressive rollout horizon during training. Early training uses short rollouts (1-2 frames of self-generated context) with mostly ground-truth conditioning, progressively expanding to full self-generated rollouts as the model matures. We formalize this as a scheduled mixing curriculum: at training step t, the rollout length L(t) increases according to a learned or predefined schedule based on a quality proxy metric (e.g., FVD on held-out clips). We additionally propose adaptive gradient truncation that adjusts truncation depth based on current rollout length, and a contrastive temporal consistency loss that penalizes drift between adjacent windows in the rolling KV cache. Experiments: We evaluate on UCF-101, Kinetics-600, and WebVid-10M, measuring training stability (loss curves, gradient norms), generation quality (FVD, FID) at varying sequence lengths (16 to 512 frames), and compare against vanilla Self Forcing and scheduled sampling baselines.

title: Adaptive KV Cache Compression for Long-Horizon Autoregressive Video Diffusion via Temporal Saliency Pruning
description:
Problem: Self Forcing's rolling KV cache mechanism enables video extrapolation but faces a fundamental memory-quality tradeoff: retaining all past KV states grows linearly with sequence length, while aggressive fixed-window truncation loses critical long-range temporal context (scene continuity, character consistency, narrative coherence) essential for long-horizon video generation.

Proposed Method: We introduce Temporal Saliency Pruning (TSP), a learned adaptive compression strategy for the rolling KV cache. TSP trains a lightweight attention-based scoring network that evaluates cached frame representations and dynamically retains high-salience keyframes (scene transitions, unique objects, character appearances) while discarding redundant intermediate frames. Rather than fixed rolling windows, TSP maintains a variable-size compressed cache with a bounded memory budget. We additionally propose a hierarchical cache structure with 'anchor frames' at coarse temporal resolution and 'detail frames' near the current generation step, enabling both long-range coherence and local smoothness. TSP is trained end-to-end within the Self Forcing paradigm using a temporal consistency auxiliary loss.

Experiments: (1) Long-video benchmarks (1000+ frames) measuring temporal consistency via DINO feature drift; (2) Ablations on cache budget vs. quality tradeoffs; (3) Comparisons against fixed-window rolling cache and uniform subsampling; (4) User studies on narrative coherence in 60-second generated videos; (5) Memory/latency profiling on single GPU.

title: Hierarchical Self Forcing: Multi-Scale Temporal Consistency via Dual-Level Autoregressive Rollout
description: Problem: Self Forcing addresses frame-level exposure bias but ignores higher-level temporal coherence — long-range narrative consistency (scene transitions, persistent object identity, global motion trends) degrades as generated sequences grow longer, since the KV cache only captures local context implicitly. Individual frame quality may be high while the video drifts semantically over extended generation. Proposed Method: We introduce Hierarchical Self Forcing, which operates autoregressive rollout at two temporal scales simultaneously. A fine-scale rollout (identical to Self Forcing) generates individual frames conditioned on a rolling KV cache of recent frames. In parallel, a coarse-scale latent summarizer compresses every N generated frames into a compact 'scene embedding' via a lightweight temporal transformer, which is injected as cross-attention context into future chunk generation. Both levels are trained end-to-end with self-generated outputs, extending the holistic video-level loss to penalize both local frame fidelity and global semantic drift (measured via CLIP embedding trajectory smoothness). Stochastic truncation is applied independently at each scale to manage backpropagation cost. Experiments: (1) Long-video generation benchmarks (>5 minutes) measuring semantic consistency, FVD, and CLIP trajectory variance; (2) Ablation of coarse-scale summarizer capacity and injection frequency; (3) Comparison with Self Forcing baseline and retrieval-augmented generation approaches on identity preservation tasks.

title: Curriculum Self Forcing: Scheduled Exposure to Self-Generated Context for Robust Long-Horizon Video Generation
description:
Problem: Self Forcing trains entirely on self-generated context from the start, which can destabilize early training when the model's outputs are extremely noisy and uninformative. Conversely, standard teacher forcing never exposes models to their own drift. A principled curriculum between these extremes could yield faster convergence and better long-horizon coherence.

Proposed Method: We introduce Curriculum Self Forcing (CSF), which interpolates between teacher forcing and full self forcing via a scheduled mixing probability. Early in training, context frames are drawn predominantly from ground-truth (high teacher-forcing ratio); as training progresses, the ratio shifts toward fully self-generated rollouts. Crucially, we parameterize the curriculum not by global training step but by predicted frame quality (measured via an online LPIPS monitor), so the schedule adapts dynamically to model capability. We additionally propose a 'partial rollout' variant where only the k most recent context frames are self-generated while older frames remain ground-truth, controlling compounding error accumulation during curriculum transitions.

Experiments: (1) Ablate curriculum schedules (linear, cosine, quality-adaptive) on FaceForensics and WebVid-10M. (2) Measure long-horizon temporal consistency (tOF, FVD) at 64, 128, 256 frame extrapolations. (3) Compare training wall-clock time to convergence vs. vanilla Self Forcing. (4) Test robustness to distribution shift via out-of-domain prompts.

title: Narrative Self Forcing: Long-Horizon Coherent Story Generation via Semantic KV Cache Compression
description: Problem: Autoregressive video diffusion models like Self Forcing excel at frame-level temporal consistency but struggle to maintain long-horizon semantic coherence—plot continuity, character identity, and scene-level narrative structure—across hundreds of generated frames, as the rolling KV cache discards distant but semantically critical context. Proposed Method: We introduce Narrative Self Forcing, which augments the rolling KV cache with a parallel 'semantic memory cache' that compresses and retains high-level narrative representations (character embeddings, scene descriptors, action states) extracted via a lightweight video-language model operating on previously generated segments. During autoregressive rollout training, both caches condition future frame generation: the rolling KV cache provides local temporal context while the semantic cache provides global narrative grounding. We train with a dual-level holistic loss: the original frame-quality loss from Self Forcing plus a novel narrative consistency loss that penalizes drift in character appearance and semantic scene continuity across distant frames. A sparse attention mechanism routes semantic queries to the appropriate cache layer. Experiments: We evaluate on long-form story generation benchmarks (StoryBench, MovieGen-Eval), measuring narrative coherence via character re-identification accuracy, scene transition smoothness, and human preference studies comparing against vanilla Self Forcing and non-causal baselines across 30-second to 3-minute generation horizons.

title: Curriculum Self Forcing: Adaptive Exposure Scheduling for Long-Horizon Autoregressive Video Generation
description: Problem: Self Forcing trains models by conditioning entirely on self-generated frames from the start, which can destabilize early training when the model's own outputs are highly noisy and uninformative. This cold-start problem may limit convergence speed and final quality, particularly for very long video sequences where compounding errors accumulate across hundreds of frames. Proposed Method: We introduce Curriculum Self Forcing (CSF), which gradually transitions the training context from ground-truth frames toward self-generated frames following a scheduled mixing policy. Specifically, we propose a token-level interpolation strategy: during training, each KV cache entry is a convex combination of the ground-truth KV vector and the self-generated KV vector, with mixing coefficient β(t) annealed from 1 (pure ground-truth) to 0 (pure self-generated) over training. We additionally propose an adaptive curriculum that adjusts β based on a running estimate of the model's current generation quality (FVD on held-out clips), accelerating annealing when quality plateaus. Planned Experiments: (1) Compare training stability and convergence curves versus vanilla Self Forcing on UCF-101 and WebVid; (2) Evaluate long-video generation quality (256+ frames) using FVD, temporal consistency metrics, and perceptual drift; (3) Ablate annealing schedules (linear, cosine, adaptive); (4) Measure computational overhead of the adaptive curriculum signal.

title: Adaptive KV Cache Compression for Long-Horizon Autoregressive Video Diffusion via Temporal Saliency Distillation
description: Problem: Self Forcing's rolling KV cache enables streaming video generation, but storing full-resolution key-value representations for all context frames creates a memory bottleneck that limits practical long-horizon generation (minutes of video). Naively evicting old cache entries degrades temporal coherence and introduces drift. Proposed Method: We introduce Temporal Saliency-Guided Cache Compression (TSCC), which learns to selectively compress and merge KV cache entries based on their predicted importance for future frame generation. A lightweight saliency predictor network—trained jointly with the video diffusion model—estimates which cached tokens are critical for maintaining global scene coherence versus local temporal consistency. High-saliency tokens are retained at full precision, while low-saliency tokens are compressed via learned vector quantization into compact 'temporal memory anchors.' We additionally distill compressed-cache generations to match full-cache quality using a temporal feature alignment loss, preventing quality degradation. Planned Experiments: (1) Long-video generation benchmarks (>1000 frames) measuring FVD, temporal consistency, and GPU memory usage versus baseline Self Forcing; (2) Ablations on compression ratios and saliency predictor architectures; (3) Scene-change stress tests measuring coherence across abrupt transitions; (4) Real-time throughput analysis on consumer-grade hardware (single RTX 4090).

title: Adaptive KV Cache Compression for Long-Horizon Autoregressive Video Diffusion via Temporal Saliency
description:
Problem: Self Forcing's rolling KV cache enables streaming video generation, but naively retaining fixed-length context windows discards potentially critical long-range temporal dependencies (e.g., scene returns, recurring characters), while storing all past context grows memory linearly and degrades efficiency for truly long videos (>1000 frames). Current rolling window approaches treat all past frames equally, losing semantically important context.

Proposed Method: We introduce Saliency-Guided Adaptive KV Compression (SAKVC), a learned mechanism that dynamically selects which past KV cache entries to retain based on a lightweight temporal saliency predictor. The predictor scores each cached frame's KV entries using cross-attention activation magnitudes from current generation steps, maintaining a compressed 'landmark buffer' of high-saliency frames alongside a standard short-term rolling window. We combine these two memory streams via learned interpolation weights during denoising, enabling both short-term coherence and long-range consistency. The saliency predictor is trained end-to-end within the Self Forcing paradigm using the same holistic video-level loss.

Experiments: (1) Long-video coherence benchmarks (VBench extended, custom 10-minute generation evaluations) measuring scene consistency and character persistence; (2) Memory-quality trade-off curves vs. fixed rolling window baselines; (3) Ablations on saliency scoring strategies; (4) Real-time throughput measurements on single GPU for 500+ frame generation.

title: Curriculum Self Forcing: Progressive Rollout Horizon Scheduling for Stable Long-Video Generation
description:
Problem: Self Forcing's autoregressive rollout during training, while addressing exposure bias, faces instability when error accumulation compounds over very long sequences (hundreds of frames). Abruptly training with full rollouts from the start leads to slow convergence and potential collapse, as gradients must propagate through long chains of stochastic diffusion steps.

Proposed Method: We introduce Curriculum Self Forcing, which gradually expands the autoregressive rollout horizon during training via a principled curriculum schedule. Initially, the model trains with short rollout windows (e.g., 2-4 frames), then progressively increases the horizon as training stabilizes. We propose three scheduling strategies: linear, exponential, and adaptive (horizon expands when validation loss plateaus). We additionally introduce a 'rollout mixing' strategy that interpolates between ground-truth and self-generated context proportionally to the current curriculum stage, creating a smooth bridge between teacher forcing and full self forcing. To handle gradient truncation more effectively under varying horizons, we derive a horizon-aware importance weighting scheme that normalizes gradient magnitudes across different rollout lengths.

Experiments: We evaluate on UCF-101, WebVid-10M, and a 1000+ frame streaming video benchmark we construct from long YouTube videos. Metrics include FVD, CLIP consistency across long sequences, error accumulation curves, and training convergence speed. Ablations compare scheduling strategies and mixing ratios against vanilla Self Forcing and standard teacher forcing baselines.

title: Adaptive KV Cache Compression for Long-Horizon Autoregressive Video Diffusion via Temporal Saliency Pruning
description:
Problem: Self Forcing's rolling KV cache enables streaming video generation, but storing and attending over all past frame KV pairs becomes a memory and compute bottleneck for very long sequences (minutes-scale video), limiting practical deployment on memory-constrained hardware. Naive fixed-window truncation loses important long-range temporal context (e.g., scene identity, character appearance), degrading consistency over extended generations.

Proposed Method: We introduce Temporal Saliency-Guided KV Compression (TSKVC), which dynamically prunes and compresses the rolling KV cache during autoregressive rollout. During training under the Self Forcing paradigm, we learn a lightweight saliency scoring network that predicts which past KV entries are most relevant to future frame generation, using attention weight statistics and a learned temporal importance predictor. Less salient entries are either evicted or merged via a learned token merging operator inspired by ToMe, while a small set of 'anchor' tokens representing scene-level context are always retained. The saliency network is trained jointly with the video diffusion model using the holistic video-level loss from Self Forcing.

Experiments: (1) Memory vs. quality trade-off on long video benchmarks (>500 frames); (2) Comparison against fixed-window rolling cache and uniform stride baselines; (3) Ablation of eviction vs. merging strategies; (4) Temporal consistency metrics (CLIP similarity, FID-vid) on minute-scale generation; (5) Throughput benchmarks on consumer GPUs.

title: Adaptive KV Cache Compression for Long-Horizon Autoregressive Video Diffusion via Temporal Saliency Routing
description: Problem: Self Forcing's rolling KV cache enables infinite video extrapolation, but uniformly storing all past frames in the cache becomes memory-prohibitive for very long sequences (minutes-scale), and naive eviction strategies (e.g., fixed window) discard temporally salient context needed for long-range coherence (consistent characters, persistent scene structure). Proposed Method: We introduce Temporal Saliency Routing (TSR), a learned cache management module that dynamically selects which KV entries to retain, compress, or evict during autoregressive rollout. TSR scores each cached frame's keys/values using a lightweight attention-based saliency predictor trained to anticipate future conditioning relevance. High-saliency entries are preserved at full resolution; medium-saliency entries are compressed via learned temporal pooling; low-saliency entries are evicted. The saliency predictor is trained jointly with the video diffusion backbone using a contrastive auxiliary loss that rewards cache configurations leading to higher future-frame generation quality. We additionally introduce a 'salient anchor' mechanism that pins globally important frames (scene transitions, key objects) indefinitely. Experiments: (1) Long-video generation benchmarks (5-30 minutes) measuring FVD, CLIP consistency, and cache memory vs. quality tradeoffs; (2) Ablations comparing TSR against sliding window, random eviction, and attention-score baselines; (3) User studies on long-range temporal coherence.

title: Adaptive KV Cache Compression for Long-Horizon Autoregressive Video Diffusion via Temporal Saliency Pruning
description: Problem: Self Forcing enables streaming video generation with rolling KV caches, but as sequence length grows indefinitely (e.g., hours-long video), the fixed-size rolling cache discards older context indiscriminately, causing semantic drift and loss of long-range coherence (characters changing appearance, scene inconsistencies). Simply enlarging the cache is computationally prohibitive. Proposed Method: We introduce Temporal Saliency Pruning (TSP), a learned cache compression strategy that selectively retains the most semantically informative KV entries across the full generated history rather than using a fixed sliding window. A lightweight saliency scorer—trained jointly with the diffusion model—assigns importance weights to cached frame tokens based on their attention contribution to current frame generation. Low-salience entries are evicted or merged via token pooling, while high-salience entries (e.g., establishing shots, character introductions) are preserved indefinitely in a compact 'episodic memory' tier. The two-tier cache (short-term rolling + long-term episodic) is differentiable and trained end-to-end within the Self Forcing framework using the same holistic video-level loss. Experiments: We evaluate on long-form video benchmarks (>5 minutes) measuring semantic consistency (CLIP cosine similarity across distant frames), FVD, and inference latency/memory versus cache size, comparing against naive rolling cache, random eviction, and attention-score baselines.

title: Hierarchical Self Forcing: Multi-Scale KV Cache Rollout for Long-Horizon Coherent Video Generation
description:
Problem: While Self Forcing effectively addresses exposure bias for short autoregressive video segments, long-horizon video generation (minutes-scale) still suffers from semantic drift and content inconsistency — the rolling KV cache discards distant context, causing the model to lose track of global scene structure, character identity, and narrative coherence over extended sequences.

Proposed Method: We introduce Hierarchical Self Forcing, which augments the frame-level KV cache rollout with a second-level 'semantic memory' cache operating at a coarser temporal scale. Specifically, we maintain two caches: (1) a local rolling KV cache for fine-grained temporal coherence (as in Self Forcing), and (2) a compressed global cache built by applying a learned temporal pooling operator over keyframe embeddings extracted every N frames. During training, self-forcing rollouts propagate gradients through both cache levels simultaneously, with stochastic truncation applied independently at each scale. A cross-attention gating mechanism learns to blend local and global context adaptively per frame. We additionally introduce a 'semantic consistency loss' that penalizes drift in DINO/CLIP feature space across distant frames.

Experiments: (1) Long-video generation benchmarks (EvalCrafter long-form, VBench extended); (2) Identity preservation metrics across 500+ frame sequences; (3) Ablations on cache hierarchy depth, pooling operators, and truncation strategies; (4) Human evaluation on narrative coherence. Baselines include vanilla Self Forcing, StreamingT2V, and non-causal long-video models.

title: Adaptive KV Cache Compression for Long-Horizon Autoregressive Video Diffusion via Temporal Saliency Distillation
description:
Problem: Self Forcing's rolling KV cache enables streaming video generation, but fixed-size cache eviction strategies discard temporal context indiscriminately, causing semantic drift and visual inconsistency in very long video sequences (>1000 frames). Naive cache management fails to distinguish between high-saliency keyframes that anchor scene identity and low-saliency transitional frames that can be safely compressed or discarded.

Proposed Method: We introduce Saliency-Guided KV Cache Compression (SGKCC), a learned cache management policy trained alongside the Self Forcing paradigm. A lightweight temporal saliency network scores each cached key-value pair based on (1) semantic importance estimated via cross-attention entropy to future frames, (2) motion magnitude, and (3) recency. High-saliency entries are preserved at full precision; low-saliency entries undergo token merging (ToMe-style) before eviction. We further introduce a distillation loss that penalizes the divergence between attention patterns computed over the compressed cache versus the full cache, ensuring the compressed representation faithfully approximates long-range context.

Experiments: (1) Long-video consistency benchmarks (VBench-Long) measuring scene coherence over 500-2000 frames; (2) Ablation of saliency scoring components; (3) Memory-quality Pareto curves comparing fixed vs. adaptive cache sizes; (4) Real-time streaming latency on single GPU across varying sequence lengths; (5) Human preference studies on narrative consistency in 60-second generated clips.

title: Curriculum Self Forcing: Progressive Exposure Bias Correction via Scheduled Rollout Depth in Autoregressive Video Diffusion
description: Problem: Self Forcing trains models by conditioning generation on their own outputs from the very beginning, but early in training the model's self-generated frames are extremely noisy and uninformative, potentially destabilizing learning. A curriculum that gradually transitions from ground-truth to self-generated context could yield faster convergence and better final quality. Method: We propose Curriculum Self Forcing, which introduces a trainable rollout depth scheduler that dynamically controls how many preceding frames come from self-generation versus ground-truth during training. Early training uses mostly ground-truth frames (shallow rollout), progressively increasing the fraction of self-generated context (deep rollout) as the model improves. We formalize this as a scheduled exposure policy parameterized by a sigmoid annealing function tied to training steps, combined with a quality-aware adaptation mechanism that uses an online FVD estimate to accelerate or decelerate the curriculum. We additionally introduce a 'mixed-context loss' weighting scheme that assigns higher gradient weight to frames generated under self-rollout context to prioritize correction of compounding errors. Experiments: We evaluate on UCF-101, Kinetics-600, and a long-form driving video benchmark, measuring FVD, training wall-clock time, convergence speed, and temporal consistency over 128-frame extrapolations. Ablations isolate annealing schedule shape, quality-aware adaptation, and mixed-context loss contributions against vanilla Self Forcing baselines.

title: Adaptive KV Cache Compression for Long-Horizon Autoregressive Video Diffusion via Temporal Saliency Distillation
description:
Problem: While Self Forcing enables efficient autoregressive video generation with rolling KV caches, long-horizon generation (minutes-scale video) remains bottlenecked by memory constraints as the rolling cache must retain sufficient temporal context. Naively truncating old cache entries discards potentially critical scene-level information (lighting, persistent objects, character appearances), leading to temporal inconsistency over extended sequences.

Proposed Method: We introduce Saliency-Guided Cache Distillation (SGCD), which learns to compress older KV cache entries rather than dropping them. A lightweight temporal saliency network scores each cached frame's keys/values by their predicted influence on future generation quality, using gradient-based attribution signals computed during Self Forcing training rollouts. High-saliency entries are retained at full resolution; low-saliency entries are compressed via learned token merging (inspired by ToMe) into compact summary tokens. A distillation objective encourages the compressed cache representation to produce generation outputs indistinguishable from full-cache generation.

Experiments: (1) Long-video consistency benchmarks (>256 frames) measuring scene coherence metrics (CLIP similarity, DINO feature drift); (2) Memory-quality Pareto curves vs. fixed-window rolling cache baselines; (3) Ablations on saliency scoring strategies (gradient-based vs. attention-based vs. recency); (4) Human evaluation on minute-long generated videos for temporal coherence. Target domains: open-domain and egocentric video generation.

title: Adaptive KV Cache Compression for Long-Horizon Autoregressive Video Diffusion via Temporal Saliency
description:
Problem: Self Forcing's rolling KV cache enables long video extrapolation, but naively retaining fixed-size temporal windows discards potentially critical long-range context (scene cuts, recurring objects, causal events) while wasting capacity on redundant frames. This causes quality degradation in videos requiring long-range temporal coherence beyond the cache window.

Proposed Method: We introduce Temporal Saliency-Guided KV Cache Compression (TS-KVC), a learned cache management strategy that dynamically selects which past frame KV entries to retain or evict based on their predicted relevance to future generation. A lightweight saliency predictor (small transformer head) operates on cached KV attention statistics during training rollouts to score each frame's contextual importance. High-salience frames (scene anchors, motion keyframes) are retained at full resolution, while low-salience frames are either evicted or compressed via learned temporal pooling. The saliency predictor is trained jointly with the video diffusion model via a contrastive auxiliary loss that rewards cache configurations producing higher video-level quality.

Experiments: (1) Long-video coherence benchmarks (>5 minutes) measuring scene consistency and object permanence; (2) Ablation comparing fixed rolling window vs. saliency-guided eviction strategies; (3) Memory-quality Pareto curves across cache sizes; (4) User study on perceptual temporal coherence for 500-frame extrapolations; (5) Generalization to multi-scene narrative video datasets (ActivityNet, MovieCuts).

title: Adaptive KV Cache Compression for Long-Horizon Autoregressive Video Diffusion via Temporal Saliency Distillation
description: Problem: Self Forcing's rolling KV cache enables streaming video generation, but fixed-size cache windows discard historical context uniformly, losing semantically important long-range temporal dependencies (e.g., a character introduced 30 seconds prior reappearing). This limits coherence over very long videos without increasing memory costs. Proposed Method: We introduce Temporal Saliency Distillation (TSD), a learned cache compression mechanism that selectively retains KV entries based on their predicted future relevance rather than simple recency. A lightweight saliency scorer—trained jointly with the diffusion model—assigns importance weights to cached frame representations by comparing them against a teacher model with full (uncompressed) context access. High-saliency tokens are preserved in a compact 'episodic memory' buffer while low-saliency tokens are evicted, maintaining a fixed memory footprint. The saliency scorer is trained via distillation: the student (compressed cache) minimizes divergence from the teacher (full cache) denoising distributions. We additionally incorporate a retrieval mechanism that re-fetches evicted tokens when current generation context signals relevance. Experiments: (1) Long-form video coherence benchmarks (VBench-Long, custom 5-minute generation suite); (2) Ablations on cache sizes and saliency thresholds; (3) Human evaluations of character/scene consistency; (4) Comparison against uniform rolling cache and token-merging baselines across generation lengths of 64–2048 frames.

title: Adaptive KV Cache Compression for Long-Horizon Autoregressive Video Diffusion via Learned Temporal Importance Scoring
description:
Problem: Self Forcing's rolling KV cache discards temporal context using a fixed window, losing semantically critical frames from early in a video (e.g., character appearances, scene establishing shots). For long-horizon generation (minutes of video), this causes semantic drift and identity inconsistency that a fixed recency-based cache cannot address.

Proposed Method: We introduce Learned Temporal Importance Scoring (LTIS), a lightweight attention-based module trained alongside the diffusion backbone that assigns importance scores to cached KV entries based on three signals: (1) semantic novelty (how much the frame diverges from its neighbors), (2) causal influence (gradient-based estimation of how much past frames influenced recent generation quality), and (3) recency decay. Rather than evicting the oldest cache entries, LTIS maintains a compressed but semantically diverse rolling cache of fixed memory budget by selectively retaining high-importance frames. The importance scorer is trained end-to-end using the same Self Forcing holistic video-level loss, creating a joint objective that rewards both generation quality and informative cache retention.

Experiments: (1) Long-horizon generation benchmarks (>300 frames) measuring semantic consistency via DINO feature drift and face re-identification accuracy. (2) Fixed GPU memory ablations comparing LTIS vs. recency-only vs. keyframe-heuristic cache eviction. (3) Human evaluation studies on narrative coherence for story-driven video generation. (4) Efficiency analysis on cache hit rates and latency overhead of the importance scorer.

title: Curriculum Self Forcing: Progressive Exposure Bias Correction via Scheduled Rollout Depth for Long-Horizon Video Generation
description: Problem: Self Forcing addresses exposure bias by conditioning on self-generated frames during training, but applying full autoregressive rollout from the start creates a challenging optimization landscape—early training produces very noisy self-generated context, making gradient signals unreliable and potentially destabilizing training. This is analogous to the cold-start problem in reinforcement learning. Proposed Method: We introduce Curriculum Self Forcing, which gradually transitions from ground-truth conditioning to fully self-generated conditioning by scheduling the rollout depth as a function of training progress. Early training uses predominantly ground-truth context with occasional self-generated frames; later training increases the fraction of self-generated context frames. We formalize this as a stochastic mixture policy where the probability of sampling self-generated vs. ground-truth context follows an annealed schedule (linear, cosine, or adaptive based on validation metrics). We further propose an 'error injection' technique that augments ground-truth frames with controlled noise calibrated to match the model's current generation error distribution, bridging the gap during curriculum transitions. Experiments: We evaluate on UCF-101, Kinetics, and a long-horizon driving dataset (nuScenes), measuring FVD, temporal consistency, and extrapolation quality at 16, 32, 64, and 128 frames. We compare against vanilla Self Forcing, DAGGER-style approaches, and ablate schedule shapes and error injection strategies, demonstrating faster convergence and improved long-horizon coherence.

title: Curriculum Self Forcing: Adaptive Exposure Scheduling for Long-Horizon Video Generation
description: Problem: Self Forcing commits fully to using self-generated context during training, which can cause instability early in training when model outputs are very poor, leading to compounding errors that destabilize gradient signals and slow convergence. A principled curriculum that gradually transitions from ground-truth to self-generated context could improve training stability and final generation quality, especially for very long video sequences where error accumulation is most severe. Method: We propose Curriculum Self Forcing, which introduces an adaptive exposure schedule that interpolates between ground-truth conditioning (teacher forcing) and fully self-generated conditioning (self forcing) throughout training. Specifically, we parameterize a per-frame mixing probability that determines whether each context frame comes from ground truth or the model's own rollout, annealing from pure teacher forcing toward pure self forcing based on a curriculum tied to validation quality metrics (e.g., FVD plateau detection). We augment this with a frame-level difficulty estimator that applies harder self-forcing earlier to temporally proximate frames (where model quality is higher) and delays it for distant frames. Experiments: We evaluate on UCF-101, Kinetics-600, and a long-horizon driving video benchmark, measuring FVD, training convergence speed, and temporal consistency at 64, 128, and 256 frame horizons. Ablations compare linear, cosine, and adaptive curriculum schedules against vanilla Self Forcing and teacher forcing baselines.

title: Curriculum Self Forcing: Adaptive Exposure Scheduling for Long-Horizon Video Generation
description:
Problem: Self Forcing commits fully to self-generated context from the start of training, which can destabilize early training when the model's outputs are extremely noisy and uninformative. Conversely, standard teacher forcing never exposes the model to its own errors. A principled curriculum between these extremes could accelerate convergence and improve long-horizon coherence beyond what either extreme achieves.

Proposed Method: We introduce Curriculum Self Forcing (CSF), which dynamically interpolates between ground-truth context and self-generated context throughout training using a scheduled mixing probability p(t). Early in training, p is low (mostly teacher forcing); as training progresses and model quality improves, p increases toward 1 (full self forcing). Crucially, we make p adaptive rather than fixed-schedule: we estimate the current model's generation quality via a lightweight discriminator score on held-out clips and use it as a feedback signal to modulate p automatically. We also extend this curriculum to the KV cache rollout depth, gradually increasing the number of autoregressive steps used during training as stability improves.

Experiments: (1) Compare CSF against pure teacher forcing, pure self forcing, and linear/cosine fixed schedules on UCF-101 and WebVid using FVD and temporal consistency metrics. (2) Ablate adaptive vs. fixed scheduling. (3) Evaluate long-horizon extrapolation (256+ frames) to test whether curriculum training reduces error accumulation. (4) Measure training wall-clock time to convergence.

title: Curriculum Self Forcing: Adaptive Exposure Scheduling for Long-Horizon Video Coherence
description: Problem: While Self Forcing eliminates exposure bias by conditioning on self-generated frames during training, it immediately forces the model to condition on fully noisy self-outputs from the start of training, creating an excessively difficult optimization landscape. This can lead to slow convergence and degraded long-range temporal coherence in very long video generation (hundreds of frames), where early errors compound severely. Proposed Method: We introduce Curriculum Self Forcing (CSF), which gradually transitions the conditioning context from ground-truth frames to self-generated frames via a learnable mixing schedule. Specifically, we parameterize a frame-level interpolation coefficient alpha(t, step) that blends ground-truth KV cache entries with self-generated ones, annealing from alpha=0 (pure ground-truth) to alpha=1 (full self-forcing) based on training progress and per-frame temporal distance. We additionally introduce a 'coherence discriminator' trained adversarially to detect temporal inconsistencies across frame windows, providing an auxiliary signal beyond the holistic video-level loss. Experiments: (1) Compare convergence speed and FVD on UCF-101 and OpenDV-YouTube against vanilla Self Forcing; (2) Evaluate 500-frame generation coherence using CLIP-based temporal consistency metrics; (3) Ablate the annealing schedule shape (linear, cosine, exponential); (4) Test generalization to audio-conditioned video generation for embodied navigation scenarios.

title: Contrastive Self Forcing: Exposure-Bias-Aware Training for Consistent Long-Horizon Video Generation via Negative Rollout Supervision
description: Problem: Self Forcing addresses exposure bias by conditioning on self-generated frames during training, but the holistic video-level loss still primarily optimizes for pixel-fidelity. For long-horizon generation (100+ frames), semantic drift and identity inconsistency compound over time in ways that frame-level or short-window losses fail to capture—characters change appearance, scenes shift implausibly, and temporal storylines lose coherence. Proposed Method: We introduce Contrastive Self Forcing (CSF), which augments the Self Forcing framework with a contrastive temporal consistency objective. During autoregressive rollout training, we maintain two parallel rollout branches: (1) the standard self-generated branch and (2) a 'corrupted' branch where a subset of KV cache entries are replaced with out-of-context frames from other videos. A temporal contrastive loss trains the model to maximize similarity of latent representations along the consistent branch while repelling the corrupted branch, explicitly reinforcing global semantic coherence without requiring external discriminators. We additionally propose a hierarchical KV cache that stores compressed semantic summaries at multiple temporal scales, allowing the model to reference both local motion context and long-range scene identity. Experiments: We evaluate on long-horizon benchmarks (UCF-101 extended, Kinetics-700 continuation tasks, custom 5-minute generation), measuring FVD, semantic identity consistency (CLIP score over time), and human preference studies, comparing against Self Forcing and non-causal baselines.

title: Adaptive KV Cache Compression for Long-Horizon Autoregressive Video Diffusion via Temporal Saliency Gating
description:
Problem: Self Forcing's rolling KV cache enables efficient streaming video generation, but as sequences grow longer (minutes-scale video), the fixed-size rolling window either discards temporally distant but semantically critical context (e.g., a character introduced early) or becomes prohibitively large, degrading coherence and memory efficiency simultaneously.

Proposed Method: We introduce Temporal Saliency Gating (TSG), a learned mechanism that dynamically compresses the KV cache by distinguishing between transient local context (recent motion dynamics) and persistent global context (scene identity, characters, long-term plot). TSG trains a lightweight attention-based saliency predictor alongside the video diffusion backbone under the Self Forcing paradigm. High-saliency tokens are retained at full resolution in a persistent memory bank; low-saliency tokens are compressed via learned vector quantization. During rollout, the model attends to both the rolling short-term cache and the compressed persistent bank, maintaining coherence across arbitrarily long sequences without linear memory growth.

Experiments: (1) Long-horizon video generation benchmarks (>5 minutes) evaluating FVD and CLIP-based semantic consistency scores. (2) Memory/latency profiling vs. fixed rolling window and full-history baselines. (3) Ablations on saliency threshold, quantization codebook size, and persistent bank capacity. title: Adaptive KV Cache Compression for Long-Horizon Autoregressive Video Diffusion via Temporal Saliency Pruning
description:
Problem: Self Forcing's rolling KV cache mechanism enables streaming video generation, but as sequences grow longer (e.g., minutes of video), the fixed-size rolling cache discards frames uniformly regardless of their semantic importance, losing critical scene context (e.g., characters, consistent backgrounds) while retaining redundant near-duplicate frames. This leads to semantic drift and inconsistency over long horizons.

Proposed Method: We introduce Temporal Saliency-Guided KV Cache Compression (TSG-Cache), a dynamic cache management strategy that selectively retains KV entries based on their predicted influence on future frame generation. We compute per-frame saliency scores using attention entropy across cached tokens during training rollouts, training a lightweight predictor to estimate which cached frames will receive high cross-attention from future frames. The cache maintains a hybrid structure: a dense recent window (last N frames) plus a sparse long-term memory of high-saliency keyframes selected by the predictor. We jointly train the saliency predictor with the video diffusion model using a distillation objective against an oracle full-cache baseline.

Experiments: (1) Long-video consistency benchmarks (>500 frames) measuring CLIP-based semantic coherence; (2) Ablations comparing uniform rolling, random sparse, and saliency-guided cache strategies; (3) User studies on narrative consistency for 60-second generated clips; (4) Efficiency analysis: cache size vs. quality trade-offs on a single GPU.

title: Adaptive KV Cache Compression for Long-Horizon Autoregressive Video Diffusion via Temporal Saliency Gating
description: Problem: Self Forcing's rolling KV cache enables efficient autoregressive video extrapolation but treats all cached frame representations equally, leading to redundant memory usage and computational overhead as sequences grow longer. For applications requiring minutes-long coherent video (e.g., autonomous driving simulation, long-form storytelling), the fixed rolling window discards potentially important distant context while wasting capacity on redundant nearby frames. Proposed Method: We introduce Temporal Saliency Gating (TSG), a learned compression module that dynamically allocates KV cache budget based on estimated temporal relevance. TSG uses a lightweight attention-based predictor trained jointly with the video diffusion model to score each cached frame's informativeness for future generation. Frames are assigned to one of three tiers: full-resolution KV retention, compressed token summarization via learned pooling, or eviction. The predictor is trained end-to-end within the Self Forcing paradigm using a auxiliary consistency loss that measures generation quality degradation when frames are compressed. Experiments: (1) Long-video generation benchmarks (>128 frames) measuring FVD, temporal consistency, and memory footprint versus fixed rolling window; (2) Ablations on cache budget allocation strategies; (3) Domain transfer to autonomous driving (nuScenes) and egocentric activity videos; (4) Real-time latency profiling showing sub-linear memory scaling with sequence length.

title: Adaptive KV Cache Compression for Long-Horizon Autoregressive Video Diffusion via Temporal Saliency Routing
description:
Problem: Self Forcing's rolling KV cache enables streaming video generation, but uniformly retaining recent context frames ignores the non-uniform temporal importance of past frames. For long-horizon video generation (minutes-scale), irrelevant recent frames crowd out semantically critical distant frames (scene-setting shots, character introductions), causing coherence degradation and wasted memory bandwidth.

Proposed Method: We introduce Saliency-Routed KV Compression (SRKC), a learned cache management policy trained jointly with the autoregressive diffusion model. A lightweight temporal saliency scorer attends over the current KV cache to predict per-frame retention scores, then dynamically allocates cache slots via a differentiable top-k selection across the entire history rather than a fixed rolling window. Frames deemed salient (scene boundaries, motion anchors) are compressed via token merging (ToMe) at reduced resolution, while recent frames remain at full resolution. The saliency scorer is trained end-to-end using the same Self Forcing holistic video loss, encouraging cache policies that maximize long-range coherence.

Experiments: (1) Long-video generation benchmarks (>256 frames) measuring scene consistency via CLIP cosine similarity over temporal gaps; (2) Memory-quality Pareto curves vs. fixed rolling cache baselines; (3) Ablations on saliency scoring architectures and compression ratios; (4) Human evaluation on narrative coherence for minute-long generated videos.

title: Curriculum Self Forcing: Adaptive Exposure Scheduling for Long-Horizon Consistent Video Generation
description: Problem: Self Forcing trains with full autoregressive rollout from the start, which can lead to unstable training dynamics early on when the model's self-generated frames are extremely noisy. Additionally, extremely long videos (thousands of frames) still suffer from accumulated drift in semantic consistency (scene layout, character identity, lighting) that a flat video-level loss does not explicitly penalize. Method: We propose Curriculum Self Forcing, which gradually transitions from ground-truth conditioning to fully self-generated conditioning during training via an adaptive schedule tied to a consistency quality signal. We introduce a dual-level loss: (1) the existing frame-quality loss and (2) a long-range semantic consistency loss computed via a frozen CLIP/DINO encoder that penalizes cosine distance drift between frame embeddings across distant temporal positions in the rollout. The curriculum schedule monitors the consistency loss and automatically controls the ground-truth mixing ratio—starting teacher-forced and annealing toward full self-forcing only as semantic coherence stabilizes. We also introduce a hierarchical KV cache with separate short-term (fine detail) and long-term (compressed semantic) memory slots to efficiently maintain global context over thousands of frames. Experiments: We evaluate on UCF-101, Kinetics-600, and long-horizon generation benchmarks (>500 frames), measuring FVD, temporal consistency scores, identity preservation metrics, and training stability curves compared to vanilla Self Forcing and scheduled sampling baselines.

title: Scheduled Self Forcing: Curriculum-Based Exposure Bias Reduction for Long-Horizon Video Generation
description: Problem: Self Forcing fully commits to self-generated context from the start of training, which can destabilize learning when the model's early outputs are extremely noisy. This cold-start problem limits how aggressively the technique can be applied to very long video sequences where compounding errors accumulate across many frames. Proposed Method: We introduce Scheduled Self Forcing, a curriculum training strategy that gradually transitions the context conditioning from ground-truth frames to self-generated frames over the course of training. Inspired by scheduled sampling in RNNs, we parameterize a mixing probability p(t) that starts near 1.0 (ground-truth dominant) and decays toward 0.0 (fully self-generated) following an adaptive schedule tied to the model's current generation quality as measured by an online FVD proxy. We further propose 'ancestry-aware truncation,' where gradient truncation depth scales with the mixing ratio, preserving more backpropagation paths through self-generated contexts as the model matures. Planned Experiments: (1) Compare scheduled vs. abrupt self forcing on UCF-101, Kinetics-600, and a long-horizon driving dataset across FVD, frame consistency, and temporal coherence metrics; (2) Ablate schedule shapes (linear, cosine, adaptive); (3) Evaluate stability during training via loss curve variance; (4) Test extrapolation to 10x training length sequences to measure error accumulation rates compared to vanilla Self Forcing.

title: Scheduled Self Forcing: Curriculum-Based Exposure Bias Mitigation for Long-Horizon Video Generation
description: Problem: Self Forcing fully commits to self-generated context during training, which can cause unstable early training dynamics since the model must simultaneously learn to generate plausible frames and handle its own noisy outputs. This cold-start problem may limit generation quality for very long sequences where compounding errors accumulate aggressively. Proposed Method: We introduce Scheduled Self Forcing, which interpolates between ground-truth conditioning and self-generated conditioning via a learnable curriculum schedule. Specifically, we define a mixing probability p(t) that starts near 1.0 (ground-truth context) and anneals toward 0.0 (fully self-generated context) over training. Rather than a fixed annealing schedule, we propose an adaptive curriculum controller that monitors a proxy metric—KL divergence between the distribution of self-generated latents and ground-truth latents—and automatically adjusts the mixing rate to maintain a target divergence gap. Additionally, we introduce a 'consistency regularization' term that penalizes large distributional shifts between consecutive frames, acting as a stabilizer during the transition from teacher-forced to self-forced regimes. Experiments: We evaluate on UCF-101, Kinetics-600, and long-horizon driving video benchmarks (nuScenes), measuring FVD, temporal consistency, and generational stability at 64, 128, and 256 frame horizons, comparing against vanilla Self Forcing, DDIM-based scheduled sampling, and DAgger-style approaches.

title: Curriculum Self Forcing: Progressive Exposure Bias Correction via Scheduled Autonomy in Autoregressive Video Diffusion
