description: Problem: Self Forcing trains models entirely on self-generated context from the start, which can be destabilizing early in training when generated frames are highly noisy and dissimilar to ground truth. This creates a challenging optimization landscape, potentially leading to slow convergence or mode collapse. A curriculum approach that gradually transitions from ground-truth conditioning to self-generated conditioning could stabilize training while preserving the inference-time benefits of Self Forcing. Proposed Method: We introduce Curriculum Self Forcing (CSF), which schedules a mixing probability p(t) that interpolates between ground-truth frames and self-generated frames as context throughout training. Early training uses mostly ground-truth context (low exposure bias correction), progressively shifting to fully autonomous rollout. We parameterize p(t) using several schedules (linear, cosine, step-wise) and additionally introduce per-frame autonomy scheduling, where earlier frames in a sequence transition to self-conditioning faster than later frames. We further combine this with a teacher-student distillation objective where a frozen checkpoint acts as a soft target to regularize the rapidly changing self-generated distribution. Experiments: We evaluate on UCF-101, Kinetics-600, and WebVid-10M, measuring FVD, training stability curves, convergence speed, and long-horizon extrapolation quality at 128+ frames, comparing against vanilla Self Forcing and scheduled sampling baselines from sequence modeling literature.

title: Adaptive KV Cache Compression for Long-Horizon Autoregressive Video Diffusion via Temporal Saliency Routing
description: Problem: Self Forcing's rolling KV cache enables long video generation but treats all cached frames equally, causing memory bottlenecks and quality degradation as sequence length grows. Critical motion context from distant frames is discarded uniformly, while redundant static background frames consume disproportionate cache space. Proposed Method: We introduce Temporal Saliency Routing (TSR), a learned compression mechanism that dynamically allocates KV cache budget based on estimated temporal importance. A lightweight saliency predictor, trained jointly with the diffusion backbone, assigns retention scores to cached frame tokens by attending to optical flow magnitudes, semantic novelty (measured via cosine distance from recent frames), and cross-attention activation patterns within the denoising UNet. High-saliency frames retain full KV representations while low-saliency frames are compressed via learned token merging (inspired by ToMe). The saliency predictor is trained end-to-end using a contrastive objective: retained frames should maximally improve generation quality measured by LPIPS on held-out future frames versus dropped frames. Experiments: (1) Memory-quality Pareto curves on UCF-101 and Kinetics-600 for 60-second+ video generation; (2) Ablation of saliency signals (flow vs. semantic vs. attention); (3) Human evaluation on long-form narrative video coherence; (4) Comparison against uniform cache eviction and recency-biased baselines; (5) Latency profiling on single GPU showing maintained real-time streaming.

title: Exposure Bias Correction for Autoregressive Video Diffusion via Adversarial Self-Distillation
description: Problem: Self Forcing addresses exposure bias through rollout-based training with truncated gradients, but the stochastic gradient truncation introduces optimization instability and limits long-horizon temporal consistency. As sequences grow longer, compounding errors from early frames degrade quality in ways that truncated backpropagation cannot fully correct. Proposed Method: We propose Adversarial Self-Distillation (ASD), which augments the Self Forcing framework with a lightweight temporal discriminator that operates on rolling windows of self-generated frames. Rather than relying solely on diffusion reconstruction loss at the video level, ASD trains a causal discriminator to distinguish between ground-truth video segments and autoregressive rollouts, providing dense gradient signal across the full sequence without requiring full backpropagation through all timesteps. The discriminator uses the same KV-cache representations from the generator, enabling efficient parameter sharing. We additionally introduce a consistency regularization term that penalizes distributional drift between frame windows, enforcing temporal coherence beyond local receptive fields. Experiments: We evaluate on UCF-101, WebVid-10M, and a long-form driving video benchmark (nuScenes), measuring FVD, temporal consistency (CLIP similarity across frames), and generation latency. Ablations compare truncated BPTT vs. ASD gradient quality, discriminator window sizes, and consistency regularization weight schedules against Self Forcing and standard autoregressive baselines.

title: Adaptive KV Cache Compression for Long-Horizon Autoregressive Video Diffusion via Temporal Saliency Routing
description:
Problem: Self Forcing's rolling KV cache enables streaming video generation, but maintaining a fixed-size cache across very long sequences forces uniform temporal forgetting, discarding potentially critical scene context (e.g., character appearances, background layouts) while retaining less informative frames. This limits coherence in minute-scale or story-driven video generation.

Proposed Method: We introduce Saliency-Routed KV Compression (SRKC), a dynamic cache management strategy that replaces the uniform rolling window with a learned temporal saliency scorer. At each generation step, a lightweight auxiliary network evaluates cached KV entries along two axes: (1) semantic importance via cross-attention activation magnitudes to current queries, and (2) recency weighting. Entries below an adaptive threshold are either evicted or compressed via low-rank factorization before archival into a compact 'long-term memory' bank. During generation, both the active rolling cache and the compressed archive are queried via approximate nearest-neighbor retrieval, enabling selective retrieval of distant but salient context.

Experiments: (1) Long-video coherence benchmarks (>300 frames) measuring character/scene consistency via DINO feature similarity; (2) Ablations on cache size vs. generation quality tradeoffs; (3) Computational profiling comparing memory footprint against vanilla Self Forcing; (4) Human evaluation of narrative coherence on story-conditioned generation tasks using a new story-video dataset derived from WebVid-Long.

title: Adaptive KV Cache Compression for Long-Horizon Autoregressive Video Diffusion via Temporal Saliency Pruning
description: Problem: Self Forcing enables real-time streaming video generation via rolling KV caches, but its fixed-size cache discards temporal context indiscriminately, causing semantic drift and temporal inconsistency in very long sequences (>1000 frames). Deciding which past frames to retain in the KV cache is a critical unsolved problem for sustained coherent video generation. Method: We propose Temporal Saliency Pruning (TSP), a learned cache management policy that dynamically scores cached key-value pairs by their predictive relevance to future frame generation. A lightweight attention-based scorer estimates each cached frame's contribution to reducing denoising loss on subsequent frames. The scorer is trained jointly with the video diffusion model using a differentiable top-k selection approximation, allowing end-to-end optimization of which context to retain. We also introduce a hierarchical cache with two tiers: a dense recent cache (last 4 seconds) and a sparse semantic cache (salient keyframes from the full history), enabling effective long-range coherence without linear memory growth. Experiments: We evaluate on UCF-101, WebVid, and a new 10-minute long-form video benchmark (YouTube timelapse/cooking sequences), measuring FVD, CLIP temporal consistency, and GPU memory usage. We compare against fixed rolling cache, uniform subsampling, and retrieval-augmented video generation baselines across sequence lengths from 128 to 10000 frames.

title: Adaptive Truncation Horizons for Self-Forcing: Learning When to Detach in Autoregressive Video Diffusion
description:
Problem: Self Forcing uses stochastic gradient truncation to manage the computational cost of autoregressive rollouts during training, but the truncation points are selected randomly rather than adaptively. This ignores the fact that different temporal positions in a video sequence contribute unequally to error accumulation — early frames where exposure bias compounds most severely may benefit from longer gradient horizons, while later frames might require shorter ones. A fixed or random truncation strategy thus wastes computation on low-signal gradients while under-investing in high-impact ones.

Proposed Method: We introduce Adaptive Truncation Horizons (ATH), which learns a lightweight truncation policy network that, given the current training state (step, frame index, rolling KV cache statistics), predicts the optimal gradient propagation depth for each training rollout. The policy is trained via a meta-gradient approach: we measure the correlation between truncated gradient estimates and full-horizon gradients on held-out mini-batches, using this signal to update the truncation policy through a bandit-style reward. We additionally propose a curriculum that gradually extends maximum allowed horizons as training stabilizes.

Experiments: We evaluate ATH on top of Self Forcing using standard benchmarks (UCF-101, Kinetics, WebVid), measuring FVD, temporal consistency, and training wall-clock time. Ablations compare random truncation, fixed truncation, and ATH at matched compute budgets, demonstrating that adaptive horizons improve generation quality and convergence speed.

title: Adaptive KV Cache Compression for Long-Horizon Autoregressive Video Diffusion via Temporal Saliency Pruning
description:
Problem: Self Forcing enables streaming video generation via rolling KV caches, but its fixed-window rolling cache discards temporally distant context uniformly, losing semantically critical information (e.g., scene anchors, character appearances) needed for long-horizon coherence. This causes gradual semantic drift in extended generations.

Proposed Method: We introduce Temporal Saliency Pruning (TSP), a learned compression strategy that replaces uniform rolling eviction with importance-aware KV cache management. A lightweight saliency network, trained jointly with the diffusion model, assigns retention scores to cached KV entries based on (1) cross-attention activation magnitude over recent frames, (2) semantic novelty relative to current context, and (3) temporal distance decay. High-salience entries (scene-establishing frames, motion pivots) are retained in a compressed long-term memory buffer using learned token merging, while low-salience entries are evicted. The saliency network is trained end-to-end using the same holistic video-level loss from Self Forcing, allowing it to discover which temporal context genuinely aids future frame quality.

Experiments: (1) Long-video generation benchmarks (>256 frames) measuring FVD and semantic consistency via CLIP similarity across distant frames; (2) Ablations comparing uniform rolling vs. TSP under equal memory budgets; (3) Memory-quality Pareto curves on a single GPU; (4) Human evaluations on narrative coherence for 60-second generated clips across diverse domains (driving, talking heads, open-world scenes).

title: Hierarchical Self Forcing: Multi-Scale Temporal Consistency for Long-Form Video Generation via Scene-Level KV Abstractions
description:
Problem: While Self Forcing addresses frame-level exposure bias through autoregressive rollout, long-form video generation (minutes-scale) still suffers from semantic drift and plot inconsistency across scenes. Current rolling KV caches discard distant context uniformly, losing high-level narrative structure even when local temporal coherence is maintained.

Proposed Method: We introduce Hierarchical Self Forcing, which augments the frame-level KV cache with a compressed scene-level abstraction cache. During training rollouts, a lightweight summarization network (small transformer) periodically distills completed scene segments into compact 'scene tokens' that encode semantic content, style, and motion statistics. These scene tokens are appended to the KV cache alongside recent frame features, providing long-range coherent conditioning without quadratic memory growth. We train the summarization network jointly using a consistency loss that penalizes semantic divergence between generated scenes and their summaries, combined with the existing holistic video-level diffusion loss. Stochastic truncation is extended to operate at both frame and scene granularities.

Experiments: (1) Long-form video generation benchmarks (FlintstonesSV, MovieGen-Bench extended to 60s clips) measuring semantic consistency via CLIP-score drift over time. (2) Ablations on cache hierarchy depth and summarization frequency. (3) User studies on narrative coherence vs. baseline Self Forcing. (4) Computational scaling analysis comparing memory vs. quality tradeoffs at varying video lengths.

title: Scheduled Self Forcing: Curriculum-Based Exposure Annealing for Long-Horizon Video Consistency
description:
Problem: Self Forcing eliminates exposure bias by always conditioning on self-generated frames during training, but this cold-start approach forces the model to immediately handle its own worst-case errors from the first training step, potentially destabilizing early training and limiting the quality of very long sequences where compounding errors accumulate. Ground-truth forcing converges quickly but generalizes poorly; self forcing generalizes well but trains slowly and struggles with early instability. There is no principled middle ground.

Proposed Method: We introduce Scheduled Self Forcing (SSF), a curriculum training paradigm that interpolates between ground-truth conditioning and self-generated conditioning via a learnable, adaptive mixing schedule. At each training step, context frames are sampled from a mixture distribution: with probability p(t) from ground truth, and 1-p(t) from self-generated rollouts, where p(t) decays from 1→0 following a schedule conditioned on current validation drift metrics. We further introduce a 'consistency discriminator' that measures temporal coherence over long rollouts and uses its signal to dynamically adjust p(t), accelerating the curriculum when the model is stable and slowing it when drift exceeds a threshold.

Experiments: (1) Compare SSF vs. pure Self Forcing and ground-truth forcing on FVD/FID at 128, 256, and 512 frame extrapolation; (2) Ablate schedule shapes (linear, cosine, adaptive); (3) Measure training stability via gradient variance across schedule strategies; (4) Evaluate on UCF-101, WebVid, and an in-house driving dataset for domain generality.

title: Curriculum Self Forcing: Adaptive Exposure Scheduling for Long-Horizon Video Generation
description: Problem: Self Forcing trains entirely on self-generated context from the start, which can destabilize early training when the model's own outputs are extremely noisy and uninformative. Conversely, gradually transitioning from ground-truth to self-generated context (curriculum learning) may allow smoother convergence and better long-horizon coherence beyond what fixed self-forcing achieves. Proposed Method: We introduce Curriculum Self Forcing, which dynamically interpolates between ground-truth context and self-generated context during training via a learnable or schedule-driven mixing probability. Specifically, at each training step we sample a 'self-forcing ratio' r ~ Beta(α_t, β_t) that determines what fraction of KV-cache entries come from self-generated vs. ground-truth frames, where α_t, β_t evolve according to a curriculum schedule tied to training progress. We additionally propose a consistency regularization term that penalizes divergence between predictions made under ground-truth context versus self-generated context, explicitly closing the train-test gap in a progressive manner. Planned Experiments: (1) Ablate curriculum schedules (linear, cosine, adaptive) on UCF-101 and WebVid-10M measuring FVD and temporal consistency. (2) Compare against vanilla Self Forcing and scheduled sampling baselines for 64-256 frame extrapolation. (3) Analyze training stability via gradient variance and loss landscape metrics. (4) Evaluate few-step distillation compatibility and latency on single-GPU streaming benchmarks.

title: Causal Consistency Forcing: Mitigating Semantic Drift in Long-Horizon Autoregressive Video Generation via Hierarchical Self-Critique
description: Problem: While Self Forcing addresses exposure bias at the frame level, long autoregressive video generation suffers from semantic drift — gradual degradation of scene coherence, character consistency, and narrative continuity over hundreds of frames. This occurs because KV cache compression loses high-level semantic context, and frame-level losses don't penalize slow semantic divergence. Proposed Method: We introduce Causal Consistency Forcing (CCF), which augments the Self Forcing framework with a hierarchical self-critique mechanism. During training rollouts, we periodically extract compact semantic summary tokens (via a frozen CLIP-based encoder) at fixed temporal intervals and inject them as additional conditioning into future frame generation. A semantic consistency discriminator, trained jointly, compares high-level embeddings of generated subsequences against a reference semantic trajectory extracted from the ground-truth video, penalizing semantic drift. We also introduce a 'consistency replay' buffer that stores and reuses previously generated keyframe embeddings during training to simulate long-context dependencies without full sequence unrolling. Experiments: We evaluate on UCF-101, Kinetics-600, and a new long-video benchmark (>500 frames) measuring FVD, semantic consistency scores (CLIP similarity over time), and character identity preservation. Ablations isolate contributions of summary tokens, semantic discriminator, and replay buffer, comparing against Self Forcing and VideoPoet baselines.

title: Adaptive KV Cache Compression for Long-Horizon Autoregressive Video Diffusion via Temporal Saliency Routing
description:
Problem: Self Forcing enables real-time streaming video generation, but its rolling KV cache discards older frames uniformly, losing important long-range temporal context (e.g., recurring characters, persistent scene structure) critical for coherent long-horizon generation spanning hundreds of seconds. Uniform eviction treats all past frames equally, causing semantic drift over extended sequences.

Proposed Method: We introduce Temporal Saliency Routing (TSR), a learned compression module that dynamically selects which KV cache entries to retain, compress, or evict based on their estimated relevance to future generation. TSR trains a lightweight attention-based saliency predictor that scores past KV entries by measuring their cross-attention activation frequency during recent denoising steps. High-saliency entries (e.g., establishing shots, key characters) are retained at full resolution; medium-saliency entries are compressed via learned token merging (similar to ToMe); low-saliency entries are evicted. The saliency predictor is trained jointly with the video diffusion model under the Self Forcing paradigm, receiving gradient signal from the holistic video-level loss.

Experiments: (1) Long-horizon video generation (>5 minutes) on UCF-101, Kinetics, and a new benchmark of procedural activity videos; (2) Ablations comparing uniform rolling cache vs. TSR at fixed memory budgets; (3) Semantic consistency metrics (character identity tracking, scene persistence scores) across temporal windows; (4) Memory-quality Pareto curves showing TSR dominates uniform eviction baselines.

title: Scheduled Self Forcing: Curriculum-Based Exposure Bias Mitigation for Long-Horizon Video Generation
description: Problem: Self Forcing fully commits to self-generated context from the start of training, which can destabilize early optimization when the model's outputs are highly noisy and unreliable. This 'cold start' problem may limit convergence speed and final quality, particularly for very long video sequences where compounding errors are severe. Proposed Method: We introduce Scheduled Self Forcing, a curriculum training strategy that interpolates between ground-truth context (teacher forcing) and self-generated context (self forcing) according to a dynamic mixing schedule. Concretely, at each training step, each KV cache frame is replaced with the self-generated equivalent with probability p(t), where p(t) follows a learned or annealed schedule that increases from 0 to 1 over training. We parameterize this schedule with a small meta-network trained via bilevel optimization to maximize held-out video quality metrics, allowing the curriculum to adapt to model capacity and dataset difficulty. Additionally, we introduce a 'worst-case rollout' sampling strategy that selects the most error-prone frames for self-conditioning, focusing the curriculum on failure modes. Experiments: We evaluate on UCF-101, Kinetics-600, and a long-horizon driving video benchmark (nuPlan), measuring FVD, temporal consistency, and compounding error growth curves across sequence lengths from 16 to 512 frames, comparing against vanilla Self Forcing, DDPM-based teacher forcing, and DAgger-style mixed training baselines.

title: Causally Consistent Long-Form Story Video Generation via Hierarchical Self-Forcing with Semantic KV Compression
description:
Problem: Autoregressive video diffusion models like Self Forcing excel at short streaming generation but struggle with long-form narrative videos (minutes-scale) where maintaining semantic consistency across distant scenes is critical. Rolling KV caches discard older context uniformly, losing important story-level information about characters, settings, and plot state.

Proposed Method: We introduce Hierarchical Self Forcing (HSF), which augments the rolling KV cache with a two-level memory: (1) a dense short-term KV cache (recent frames, as in Self Forcing) and (2) a compressed semantic long-term memory that distills past generated segments into compact learned 'episode tokens' via a trainable cross-attention summarization module. During autoregressive rollout training, both caches are populated from self-generated outputs, preserving the exposure-bias correction of Self Forcing. The summarization module is trained end-to-end with a contrastive semantic consistency loss that penalizes character/scene drift across segments, and a holistic video-level loss over the full sequence.

Experiments: (1) Long-form story video generation on ActivityNet-Captions and a new long-form benchmark derived from movie clips; (2) Ablations comparing rolling-only vs. hierarchical cache; (3) Character/scene consistency metrics (face re-ID, CLIP similarity across segments); (4) Computational cost vs. generation quality trade-offs at 1-5 minute generation lengths; (5) Human evaluation of narrative coherence.

title: Curriculum Self Forcing: Adaptive Exposure Scheduling for Long-Horizon Video Consistency
description:
Problem: Self Forcing trains autoregressive video diffusion models by conditioning on self-generated frames from the very beginning of training, which can destabilize early optimization when the model's own outputs are highly noisy. Furthermore, for very long video generation (hundreds of frames), error accumulation in the rolling KV cache remains challenging, as temporal consistency degrades over extended horizons.

Proposed Method: We introduce Curriculum Self Forcing (CSF), which gradually transitions from ground-truth conditioning to self-generated conditioning via an adaptive scheduling mechanism. Early in training, frames are conditioned on a mixture of ground-truth and self-generated context, with the mixture ratio controlled by a curriculum schedule tied to a quality signal (e.g., FVD on held-out clips). We further propose a 'temporal contrastive loss' that penalizes semantic drift across non-adjacent frame windows in the rolling KV cache, encouraging global coherence beyond local frame-to-frame consistency. Finally, we introduce a hierarchical KV cache with separate short-term (fine detail) and long-term (semantic summary) memory slots to maintain identity and scene consistency over 500+ frames.

Experiments: We evaluate on UCF-101, Kinetics-600, and a new long-video benchmark (>5 minutes) measuring FVD, temporal consistency scores, and identity preservation. Ablations compare scheduling strategies, contrastive loss variants, and cache architectures against Self Forcing and other autoregressive baselines.

title: Adaptive KV Cache Compression for Long-Horizon Autoregressive Video Diffusion via Temporal Saliency Pruning
description:
Problem: Self Forcing's rolling KV cache enables efficient video extrapolation but treats all cached frames equally, leading to memory bottlenecks and degraded coherence during very long-horizon generation (minutes of video). As sequences grow, the fixed-size cache must evict frames arbitrarily, potentially discarding semantically critical context (scene anchors, character appearances) while retaining redundant frames.

Proposed Method: We introduce Temporal Saliency-Guided KV Cache Pruning (TSKP), a learned cache management strategy that dynamically scores and selectively retains the most contextually important KV entries during autoregressive rollout. Concretely, we train a lightweight attention-based saliency predictor that estimates each cached frame's future utility by measuring its cross-attention activation magnitude against recent query frames. Frames below a learned threshold are pruned, while high-saliency frames (scene boundaries, motion pivots) are compressed via token merging rather than fully evicted. The saliency predictor is trained jointly with the video diffusion model using a contrastive objective that rewards cache configurations maintaining long-range semantic consistency.

Experiments: (1) Long-video coherence benchmarks (>500 frames) measuring identity preservation and scene consistency via CLIP similarity over time. (2) Memory vs. quality Pareto curves comparing fixed rolling cache, random eviction, and TSKP. (3) Ablations on saliency scoring strategies and compression ratios. (4) User studies on perceived temporal coherence for 60-second generated clips.

title: Curriculum Self Forcing: Adaptive Exposure Scheduling for Long-Horizon Video Consistency
description: Problem: Self Forcing eliminates exposure bias by always conditioning on self-generated frames during training, but this cold-start approach can cause training instability and slow convergence early on, since the model must simultaneously learn to generate and cope with its own errors from scratch. Long-horizon generation (hundreds of frames) further amplifies drift where small per-frame errors compound dramatically. Proposed Method: We introduce Curriculum Self Forcing, which gradually transitions training from ground-truth conditioning to fully self-generated conditioning following an adaptive schedule. Rather than a fixed annealing rate, we propose an error-aware curriculum that monitors the KV cache divergence (L2 distance between cached keys/values from ground-truth vs. self-generated contexts) and accelerates or decelerates the transition accordingly. Additionally, we introduce a temporal consistency auxiliary loss that penalizes semantic drift across distant frames using DINO feature similarity, operating on the rolling KV cache window. We also explore mixing ratios at the segment level rather than frame level to better preserve local coherence. Experiments: (1) Convergence speed and FVD on UCF-101, Kinetics-600, and OpenDV driving datasets; (2) Long-horizon stability metrics over 500+ frame generation; (3) Ablations over curriculum schedules; (4) Comparison against Self Forcing baseline and scheduled sampling baselines showing improved drift resistance under extreme extrapolation.

title: Scheduled Self Forcing: Curriculum-Based Exposure Blending for Robust Long-Horizon Video Generation
description: Problem: Self Forcing fully commits to self-generated context from the start of training, which can cause unstable optimization early on when the model's own outputs are highly noisy and misleading. This cold-start problem may limit convergence speed and final quality, particularly for very long video sequences where compounding errors are severe. Proposed Method: We introduce Scheduled Self Forcing, which interpolates between ground-truth context frames and self-generated frames during training via a curriculum schedule. Early in training, a high fraction of ground-truth frames are mixed into the KV cache alongside self-generated frames; this ratio shifts monotonically toward pure self-generated context as training progresses. We parameterize the mixing probability with multiple schedule shapes (linear, cosine, exponential decay) and also explore frame-position-dependent mixing, where earlier frames in the context window retain ground-truth longer. We further propose an adaptive schedule controller that dynamically adjusts the mixing ratio based on a moving average of the holistic video-level loss, preventing premature exposure to self-generated context when loss plateaus occur. Experiments: We evaluate on standard video generation benchmarks (UCF-101, Kinetics, WebVid) measuring FVD, CLIP consistency, and temporal coherence at 64+ frame horizons. Ablations compare schedule shapes, adaptive vs. fixed schedules, and extrapolation robustness over 300+ frame rollouts against vanilla Self Forcing and teacher-forcing baselines.

title: Scheduled Self Forcing: Curriculum-Based Exposure Bias Mitigation for Long-Horizon Video Generation
description: Problem: Self Forcing fully commits to self-generated context from the start of training, which can destabilize early training when the model's outputs are very noisy and uninformative. This limits scalability to very long video sequences where compounding errors in early training can collapse learning. Method: We propose Scheduled Self Forcing, a curriculum training strategy that interpolates between ground-truth context and self-generated context according to a learnable or predefined annealing schedule. Concretely, at each training step we stochastically blend KV cache entries: with probability p(t) we substitute ground-truth encoded frames, and with probability 1-p(t) we use self-generated frames, where p(t) decays from 1 to 0 following a cosine or adaptive schedule tied to the model's current generation quality (measured via an online FVD proxy). We additionally introduce a context quality conditioning signal — a scalar noise level embedding appended to KV entries — allowing the model to explicitly reason about the reliability of its context at inference time. Experiments: (1) Compare against vanilla Self Forcing on 128-frame and 512-frame generation benchmarks using FVD, temporal consistency, and training stability metrics; (2) Ablate schedule shapes and quality conditioning; (3) Evaluate on long-form video extrapolation tasks including driving and egocentric activity datasets to demonstrate reduced drift over extended horizons.

title: Reward-Guided Self Forcing: Aligning Autoregressive Video Diffusion with Human Preferences via Online Rollout Optimization
description:
Problem: While Self Forcing addresses exposure bias in autoregressive video diffusion, the training objective remains reconstruction-focused (pixel/perceptual loss), leaving a gap between generated video quality and human aesthetic preferences, temporal coherence as judged by humans, or task-specific rewards (e.g., physical plausibility, instruction following for video generation from text).

Proposed Method: We extend the Self Forcing framework by replacing or augmenting the holistic video-level loss with differentiable or REINFORCE-style reward signals from pretrained reward models (e.g., VideoScore, temporal consistency classifiers, or CLIP-based text-video alignment scores). Because Self Forcing already performs full autoregressive rollouts during training with KV caching, we can directly compute sequence-level rewards on these rollouts and backpropagate through stochastic gradient truncation—analogous to RLHF but operating natively in the autoregressive diffusion rollout regime. We introduce a mixed objective combining the original reconstruction loss with a reward-weighted policy gradient term and an entropy regularizer to prevent reward hacking.

Experiments: (1) Ablations comparing reconstruction-only vs. reward-augmented training on UCF-101 and WebVid; (2) Human preference studies evaluating temporal coherence and text alignment; (3) Scaling reward diversity (aesthetic, motion smoothness, text-video alignment); (4) Analysis of reward hacking via truncation length and entropy regularization; (5) Downstream task evaluation on instruction-conditioned video generation benchmarks.

title: Temporal Consistency Under Distribution Shift: Adaptive KV Cache Correction for Long-Horizon Autoregressive Video Diffusion
description: Problem: Self Forcing mitigates exposure bias via autoregressive rollout during training, but in very long video generation (hundreds of frames), accumulated errors in the rolling KV cache cause semantic drift—characters change appearance, scenes lose coherence, and physics become inconsistent. The rolling window discards distant context abruptly, losing long-range dependencies critical for narrative consistency. Proposed Method: We introduce Adaptive Cache Correction (ACC), a lightweight auxiliary module that periodically detects and corrects distributional drift in the KV cache. ACC consists of: (1) a drift detector that computes feature-space divergence between current cached representations and a compressed long-term memory bank using exponential moving averages; (2) a cache correction network that injects corrective residuals into stale KV entries when drift exceeds a threshold; and (3) a hierarchical memory structure maintaining both a short-term rolling window and a compressed long-term summary updated via learned attention pooling. ACC is trained jointly with the base autoregressive model using a drift-aware consistency loss that penalizes semantic inconsistency between distant frames. Experiments: We evaluate on VBench, EvalCrafter, and a new Long-Video Consistency Benchmark (500+ frames) measuring character identity preservation, scene stability, and physics plausibility. Ablations compare rolling-only vs. hierarchical memory, and analyze drift correction frequency vs. computational overhead. We target maintaining generation quality beyond 10x the training sequence length.

title: Critic-Guided Self Forcing: Leveraging Discriminative Feedback for Long-Horizon Video Coherence
description:
Problem: While Self Forcing addresses exposure bias through autoregressive rollout during training, the holistic video-level loss still relies on diffusion reconstruction objectives that may not capture high-level semantic coherence (scene consistency, object permanence, narrative continuity) over very long sequences (>100 frames). Frame-level and even short-clip-level losses can miss slow-drift artifacts that accumulate over time.

Proposed Method: We augment Self Forcing's training pipeline with a lightweight temporal discriminator (video critic) that operates on full-length rollouts and provides reward signals targeting long-range coherence. Specifically, we train a causal transformer critic jointly with the generator using an adversarial objective over temporally-subsampled keyframes spanning the entire generated sequence. To stabilize training, we combine this adversarial signal with the original Self Forcing diffusion loss via adaptive loss weighting based on critic confidence. We further propose a 'coherence contrastive loss' that pulls together KV-cache representations of semantically related frames while pushing apart drifted representations, encouraging the rolling KV cache to maintain consistent scene context.

Experiments: (1) Long-video generation benchmarks (EvalCrafter, VBench extended to 300+ frames); (2) ablations on critic architecture and loss weighting; (3) human evaluation of semantic consistency vs. baseline Self Forcing and non-causal diffusion models; (4) measuring temporal identity drift using face/object tracking metrics across extended sequences.

title: Scheduled Self Forcing: Curriculum-Based Exposure Blending for Robust Long-Horizon Video Generation
description: Problem: Self Forcing fully commits to self-generated context from the start of training, which can destabilize early training when the model's outputs are highly noisy and far from ground truth. This abrupt switch may limit robustness to diverse generation errors and hurt long-horizon coherence beyond the training sequence length. Proposed Method: We introduce Scheduled Self Forcing, a curriculum learning framework that smoothly interpolates between teacher-forced (ground-truth context) and self-forced (model-generated context) training regimes. Specifically, we maintain a blending schedule α(t) ∈ [0,1] over training steps that controls the probability of using self-generated versus ground-truth KV cache entries per frame. We explore several schedules (linear, cosine, adversarially-adapted) and propose a mismatch-aware schedule that dynamically adjusts α based on the current frame-level perceptual distance between self-generated and ground-truth frames. Additionally, we introduce a consistency regularization term that penalizes drift in the KV cache representations across the blending boundary. Experiments: We evaluate on UCF-101, Kinetics-600, and a long-horizon driving video benchmark, measuring FVD, temporal consistency scores, and extrapolation quality at 2×, 4×, and 8× training sequence length. We compare against vanilla Self Forcing, pure teacher forcing, and DAGGER-style baselines, demonstrating faster convergence and improved long-horizon stability.

title: Adaptive KV Cache Compression for Long-Horizon Autoregressive Video Diffusion via Temporal Saliency Distillation
description:
Problem: Self Forcing's rolling KV cache enables streaming video generation, but maintaining fixed-size caches over very long sequences (minutes of video) forces uniform eviction of past context, discarding temporally critical frames (scene transitions, key objects) and degrading long-range coherence. Naive cache expansion is memory-prohibitive.

Proposed Method: We introduce Temporal Saliency-Guided KV Compression (TSC), which learns to selectively retain the most semantically important KV entries across the rolling cache. Specifically, we train a lightweight saliency predictor that scores each cached frame's KV contribution using cross-attention gradients from the denoising network, identifying which historical frames most influence current generation. High-saliency frames are retained at full precision; low-saliency frames are either evicted or compressed via learned token merging (similar to ToMe but temporally adapted). We distill the uncompressed model's attention distributions into the compressed model to preserve generation quality. The saliency predictor is jointly trained within the Self Forcing paradigm, using the holistic video-level loss to reward long-range consistency.

Experiments: (1) Long-video generation benchmarks (>500 frames) measuring FVD, scene consistency, and memory footprint; (2) Ablations on saliency scoring strategies vs. FIFO/random eviction; (3) Cache size vs. quality trade-off curves; (4) Human evaluation on narrative coherence across extended sequences. Baseline: Self Forcing with fixed rolling cache.

title: Temporal Consistency Self-Forcing: Training-Free Adaptation of Autoregressive Video Diffusion for Long-Horizon Scene Consistency via Semantic KV Cache Compression
description:
Problem: While Self Forcing addresses exposure bias and enables real-time streaming video generation, long-horizon autoregressive generation (minutes-scale) still suffers from semantic drift — gradually losing consistency in scene identity, object permanence, and lighting conditions as the rolling KV cache discards early context. The model 'forgets' what the scene looked like hundreds of frames ago.

Proposed Method: We introduce Semantic KV Cache Compression (SKCC), a training-free extension to Self Forcing's rolling cache mechanism. Rather than discarding old KV entries purely by recency (FIFO), we maintain a compressed 'semantic memory bank' that retains a small set of highly-informative key frames selected via attention entropy scoring — frames whose KV entries receive disproportionate cross-attention from recent frames. These compressed entries are periodically updated using exponential moving average fusion to prevent staleness while preserving global scene structure. The method requires no retraining and is plug-and-play with any Self Forcing checkpoint.

Experiments: (1) Long-video generation benchmarks (>500 frames) measuring scene consistency via DINO feature cosine similarity over time; (2) Ablation of cache replacement strategies (FIFO vs. entropy-guided vs. SKCC); (3) Memory/latency trade-off analysis; (4) User studies comparing perceptual temporal coherence on diverse scene types including dynamic environments and static indoor scenes.

title: Exposure Bias Correction for Autoregressive Audio-Visual Generation via Cross-Modal Self Forcing
description: Problem: Autoregressive video generation models like Self Forcing address exposure bias in the visual domain, but joint audio-visual generation systems face a compounded exposure bias problem: errors in generated video frames corrupt subsequent audio generation, and vice versa, creating cascading cross-modal drift that worsens over long sequences. Existing audio-visual generation models train on ground-truth context in both modalities, causing severe degradation at inference time. Proposed Method: We extend the Self Forcing paradigm to joint audio-visual autoregressive diffusion by introducing Cross-Modal Self Forcing (CMSF). During training, we perform synchronized autoregressive rollout where both audio spectrograms and video frames are generated from the model's own prior outputs using shared KV caches per modality. We introduce a cross-modal consistency loss that penalizes audio-visual desynchronization across the generated sequence holistically, in addition to per-modality reconstruction objectives. A cross-modal attention mechanism allows each modality's KV cache to attend to the other's cached representations, enabling coherent joint generation. Stochastic gradient truncation is applied independently per modality with coordinated scheduling to balance compute. Experiments: We train on VGGSound and AudioSet-2M, evaluating Frechet Audio Distance, FVD, audio-visual synchrony (SyncNet score), and long-sequence drift metrics up to 60-second generations, comparing against ground-truth-conditioned baselines and single-modality Self Forcing.

title: Curriculum Self Forcing: Adaptive Exposure Scheduling for Long-Horizon Autoregressive Video Generation
description:
Problem: Self Forcing trains models by always conditioning on self-generated frames from the very beginning, which may cause training instability and slow convergence when the model's early outputs are highly noisy and uninformative. For very long video sequences (hundreds of frames), compounding errors in self-generated KV caches can destabilize gradients even with truncation strategies, limiting coherent long-horizon generation.

Proposed Method: We introduce Curriculum Self Forcing, which dynamically interpolates between ground-truth conditioning and self-generated conditioning throughout training via a learnable exposure schedule. Rather than a fixed binary choice, we maintain a per-training-step mixing probability that gradually shifts from ground-truth context toward fully self-generated context following a curriculum — starting with mostly ground-truth frames and progressively increasing reliance on model rollouts as training stabilizes. Crucially, we adaptively tune this schedule using a quality signal derived from a lightweight discriminator that monitors distributional divergence between ground-truth and self-generated frame statistics, pausing curriculum advancement when instability is detected.

Experiments: (1) Compare against vanilla Self Forcing and scheduled sampling baselines on long video benchmarks (UCF-101, Kinetics, custom 500-frame sequences). (2) Measure FVD, temporal consistency, and training convergence curves. (3) Ablate curriculum shapes (linear, cosine, adaptive) and discriminator design choices. (4) Evaluate robustness to distribution shift on out-of-domain test sequences.

title: Reward-Guided Self Forcing: Aligning Autoregressive Video Diffusion with Human Preferences via Holistic Sequence-Level RLHF
description: Problem: Current autoregressive video diffusion models optimize frame reconstruction or adversarial losses, but these objectives poorly correlate with human-perceived quality attributes like aesthetic appeal, temporal coherence, and semantic faithfulness. Self Forcing's holistic video-level loss opens a natural avenue for integrating learned reward signals, but no work has explored coupling autoregressive rollout training with human preference optimization for video generation. Proposed Method: We extend Self Forcing's training paradigm by replacing (or augmenting) the video-level diffusion loss with a differentiable reward signal from a pretrained video reward model (e.g., fine-tuned VideoScore or a contrastive video-text model). During training, we perform autoregressive rollout with KV caching to generate complete sequences, score them with the reward model, and backpropagate through stochastic gradient truncation as in Self Forcing. We further introduce a KL-regularized REINFORCE objective that prevents reward hacking while preserving video diversity. A secondary contribution is a lightweight reward model trained on human preference data specifically collected for streaming/long-form video quality. Experiments: (1) Human preference studies comparing reward-guided vs. baseline Self Forcing on text-to-video benchmarks (EvalCrafter, VBench); (2) Ablations on reward model choice and KL regularization strength; (3) Temporal coherence metrics on long video extrapolation tasks; (4) Measuring diversity-quality tradeoffs.

title: Scheduled Self Forcing: Curriculum-Based Exposure Bias Correction for Long-Horizon Video Generation
description: Problem: Self Forcing commits fully to self-generated context from the start of training, which can destabilize early training when the model's outputs are highly noisy and uninformative. This cold-start problem limits how aggressively we can apply self-forcing without careful hyperparameter tuning, and becomes more pronounced for very long video sequences where error accumulation is severe. Proposed Method: We introduce Scheduled Self Forcing, a curriculum training strategy that gradually transitions the conditioning context from ground-truth frames to self-generated frames over the course of training. Concretely, we define a mixing schedule p(t) that begins at p=0 (pure teacher forcing) and anneals toward p=1 (pure self forcing), with the schedule shape (linear, cosine, exponential) treated as a hyperparameter. We additionally propose a confidence-weighted mixing strategy where the model uses ground-truth frames for timesteps where its own predicted outputs exceed a perceptual quality threshold, providing adaptive curriculum pacing per-sample. We integrate this with the rolling KV cache mechanism from Self Forcing. Experiments: We evaluate on standard video generation benchmarks (UCF-101, Kinetics, WebVid) measuring FVD, temporal consistency, and error accumulation over 100+ frame extrapolations. We compare training stability curves, convergence speed, and final generation quality against vanilla Self Forcing, showing improved long-horizon coherence with faster convergence.

title: Narrative Self Forcing: Long-Horizon Coherent Story Video Generation via Semantic KV Cache Compression
description:
Problem: Autoregressive video diffusion models like Self Forcing excel at short-horizon temporal consistency but degrade over very long sequences (hundreds of seconds) because the rolling KV cache discards distant context, causing semantic drift—characters change appearance, scene lighting becomes inconsistent, and narrative threads are lost. This is critical for story video generation where global coherence must be maintained across minutes of footage.

Proposed Method: We introduce Narrative Self Forcing, which augments the rolling KV cache with a compressed semantic memory bank. During training rollout, we periodically distill past KV states into compact 'narrative tokens' using a learned cross-attention summarization module trained jointly with the video diffusion model. These narrative tokens are injected alongside the local rolling cache, providing long-range semantic anchoring without linear memory growth. We apply Self Forcing's holistic video-level loss across both local (frame-to-frame) and global (scene-to-scene) timescales by sampling distant frame pairs during training to explicitly penalize semantic drift.

Experiments: (1) Long-form story video generation on StorySalon and a new 10-minute narrative video benchmark we curate from film datasets; (2) Ablations on narrative token count, compression ratio, and global loss weighting; (3) Character identity consistency metrics (face re-ID similarity) and scene coherence scores over time; (4) Comparison against Self Forcing baseline, StreamingT2V, and retrieval-augmented approaches.

title: Scheduled Self Forcing: Curriculum-Based Exposure Bias Mitigation for Long-Horizon Video Generation
description:
Problem: Self Forcing commits fully to self-generated context from the start of training, which can destabilize learning when the model's early outputs are extremely noisy. Conversely, standard teacher forcing never exposes the model to its own errors. A principled curriculum bridging these extremes could yield faster convergence and better long-horizon coherence.

Proposed Method: We introduce Scheduled Self Forcing (SSF), a curriculum training strategy that interpolates between teacher forcing and self forcing via a mixing schedule. At each training step, context frames are drawn from a Bernoulli mixture: with probability p(t) use ground-truth frames, with probability 1-p(t) use self-generated frames, where p(t) decays from 1 to 0 following a cosine or learned adaptive schedule. We further propose a 'difficulty-aware' scheduling variant that dynamically adjusts p(t) per video clip based on the model's current prediction uncertainty (measured via KV-cache attention entropy), applying more self-generated context on easier clips earlier. We integrate this with rolling KV caching from Self Forcing and few-step diffusion.

Experiments: (1) Compare convergence speed and final FVD/FID on UCF-101, Kinetics-600, and long-form OpenDV-YouTube against vanilla Self Forcing and teacher forcing baselines. (2) Ablate schedule shape and adaptive vs. fixed scheduling. (3) Evaluate temporal consistency over 10-minute extrapolations. (4) Measure training wall-clock time vs. generation quality tradeoff.

title: Curriculum Self Forcing: Adaptive Exposure Scheduling for Long-Horizon Video Diffusion with Compounding Error Control
description: Problem: While Self Forcing eliminates exposure bias by conditioning on self-generated frames during training, it introduces a new challenge: early in training, self-generated frames are extremely noisy, creating highly unstable gradients and slow convergence. A fixed self-forcing strategy treats all training stages equally, ignoring the curriculum nature of learning to generate coherent long videos. Compounding errors over very long sequences (100+ frames) remain problematic even with Self Forcing. Method: We propose Curriculum Self Forcing (CSF), which dynamically interpolates between ground-truth conditioning and self-generated conditioning based on a learnable curriculum scheduler. The scheduler monitors per-frame generation quality via a lightweight discriminator head and automatically increases the self-generation ratio as the model matures. Additionally, we introduce an error accumulation penalty that explicitly regularizes the KV cache representations to prevent drift across long sequences, using contrastive objectives that align cached representations between ground-truth and self-generated rollouts. We also propose a hierarchical rollout strategy where coarse temporal keyframes are generated first with full Self Forcing, while intermediate frames use partial ground-truth blending. Experiments: We evaluate on UCF-101, Kinetics-600, and a new 10-minute video benchmark measuring temporal coherence at 500+ frame horizons, comparing FVD, CLIP consistency scores, and wall-clock generation speed against Self Forcing and teacher-forcing baselines.

title: Reward-Guided Self Forcing: Aligning Autoregressive Video Diffusion with Human Preferences via Sequence-Level RLHF
description: Problem: Self Forcing introduces sequence-level training that directly evaluates entire generated videos, but its holistic loss is still based on reconstruction objectives. This leaves a gap between optimizing pixel-level fidelity and aligning generated videos with human aesthetic preferences, semantic coherence, or task-specific goals (e.g., instruction-following in text-to-video generation). Existing RLHF approaches for video diffusion apply rewards frame-wise or require expensive full-sequence rollouts incompatible with standard training pipelines. Method: We propose Reward-Guided Self Forcing, which augments the Self Forcing training paradigm with a differentiable sequence-level reward signal derived from a pretrained video reward model (e.g., VideoScore or a fine-tuned CLIP-based temporal consistency scorer). During autoregressive rollout with KV caching, we collect full generated sequences and compute reward-weighted policy gradient updates alongside the standard diffusion loss. We leverage Self Forcing's stochastic gradient truncation to make reward backpropagation computationally tractable. A KL-divergence penalty against the base model prevents reward hacking. Experiments: (1) Text-to-video alignment benchmarks (EvalCrafter, T2V-CompBench) measuring prompt adherence; (2) Human preference studies comparing against DPO-finetuned baselines; (3) Ablations on reward weighting, truncation depth, and KL penalty strength; (4) Generalization to domain-specific rewards (e.g., physics plausibility for robot manipulation videos).

title: Adaptive KV Cache Compression for Long-Horizon Autoregressive Video Diffusion via Temporal Importance Scoring
description:
Problem: Self Forcing's rolling KV cache mechanism discards context frames using a fixed window, losing potentially critical long-range temporal dependencies (e.g., scene consistency, recurring objects) needed for coherent long-horizon video generation. Naive cache expansion is prohibitive for memory and latency.

Proposed Method: We introduce a learned Temporal Importance Scoring (TIS) module that dynamically selects which KV cache entries to retain, compress, or evict based on their predicted relevance to future frame generation. Specifically, we train a lightweight attention-based scorer that, at each autoregressive step, estimates the importance of each cached frame's keys/values using a combination of: (1) query-key correlation from the current denoising step, (2) a recency bias, and (3) a semantic diversity bonus to prevent redundant retention. High-importance frames are kept at full resolution, mid-importance frames are compressed via PCA-based key-value distillation into summary tokens, and low-importance frames are evicted. The TIS module is trained end-to-end within the Self Forcing paradigm using the holistic video-level loss.

Experiments: We evaluate on long-form video generation benchmarks (>128 frames) measuring: temporal consistency (CLIP cosine similarity across distant frames), FVD, memory footprint vs. fixed rolling cache baselines, and user studies on scene coherence. Ablations compare fixed window, random eviction, recency-only, and full TIS strategies.

title: Scheduled Self Forcing: Curriculum-Based Exposure Blending for Robust Long-Horizon Video Generation
description: Problem: Self Forcing fully commits to self-generated context during training, which can destabilize early training stages when model outputs are poor, leading to compounding noise that hinders convergence. Additionally, the binary choice between ground-truth and self-generated context ignores intermediate regimes that may improve robustness to diverse inference conditions. Method: We propose Scheduled Self Forcing, which introduces a curriculum-based exposure blending strategy inspired by scheduled sampling but adapted for diffusion-based autoregressive video models. During training, each KV cache frame is stochastically replaced with either ground-truth or self-generated context according to a time-varying mixture probability that anneals from ground-truth-dominant early training toward fully self-generated context. Crucially, we parameterize the blending schedule as a function of both training step and temporal distance (frames further in the future receive more self-generated context earlier), enabling fine-grained control. We further introduce a consistency regularization term that penalizes divergence between predictions conditioned on ground-truth vs. self-generated context, enforcing robustness. Experiments: We evaluate on UCF-101, Kinetics-600, and an in-house long-video benchmark measuring FVD, temporal consistency, and drift over 100+ generated frames. Ablations compare fixed vs. adaptive schedules, and we analyze training stability via gradient norms and loss curves across curriculum variants.

title: Reward-Guided Self Forcing: Aligning Autoregressive Video Diffusion with Human Preferences via Holistic Sequence Rewards
description: Problem: While Self Forcing addresses exposure bias through video-level holistic loss, the training signal remains purely reconstruction-based and does not align generated videos with human preferences (e.g., aesthetic quality, temporal coherence, prompt faithfulness). Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) has transformed language models but remains underexplored for autoregressive video generation, partly because the sequential rollout structure makes reward propagation expensive. Proposed Method: We augment the Self Forcing framework with differentiable reward signals from pre-trained video quality models (e.g., VideoScore, CLIP-based aesthetic scorers, optical flow coherence metrics). During training rollouts with KV caching, we compute a holistic sequence reward at the end of each generated clip and backpropagate through the stochastic gradient truncation mechanism already present in Self Forcing. We additionally introduce a lightweight reward-conditioning token prepended to each chunk, allowing the model to be steered at inference time toward high-reward outputs without re-training. Planned Experiments: (1) Compare reward-guided vs. baseline Self Forcing on EvalCrafter and VBench benchmarks; (2) Ablate reward types (aesthetic, motion, text-alignment) and their combinations; (3) Measure inference-time steering quality vs. computational overhead; (4) Human preference studies comparing to non-causal diffusion baselines fine-tuned with RLHF.

title: Adaptive KV Cache Compression for Long-Horizon Autoregressive Video Diffusion via Temporal Saliency Distillation
description:
Problem: Self Forcing enables streaming video generation via rolling KV caches, but maintaining full KV cache histories across very long sequences (e.g., minutes-long videos) causes memory to grow linearly with sequence length, limiting scalability. Naively evicting old cache entries degrades temporal coherence and introduces drift in scene consistency over extended horizons.

Proposed Method: We introduce Temporal Saliency Distillation (TSD), a learned cache compression strategy that identifies which past KV cache entries are most causally influential for future frame quality. A lightweight saliency predictor network is trained jointly with the video diffusion model to score cached key-value pairs by their estimated contribution to downstream denoising loss. Low-salience entries are compressed via learned token merging (merging spatially similar tokens within a frame's cache) while high-salience entries are retained at full resolution. Additionally, we propose a distillation objective where a 'full-cache teacher' supervises a 'compressed-cache student' during Self Forcing rollout training, preserving temporal coherence signals without requiring full cache storage at inference.

Experiments: (1) Long-video generation benchmarks (UCF-101 extended, custom 2-minute driving clips) measuring FVD and scene consistency at 500+ frames. (2) Memory footprint vs. generation quality trade-off curves compared to fixed-window rolling cache baselines. (3) Ablations on saliency predictor architectures and compression ratios. (4) User studies evaluating perceptual temporal coherence over long horizons.

title: Adaptive KV Cache Compression for Long-Horizon Autoregressive Video Diffusion via Saliency-Guided Token Pruning
description: Problem: Self Forcing enables real-time autoregressive video generation via rolling KV caches, but the fixed-size rolling window discards temporal context abruptly, causing semantic drift and content inconsistency over very long video sequences (>1000 frames). Simply expanding the cache window is computationally prohibitive. Proposed Method: We introduce Saliency-Guided Cache Compression (SGCC), which dynamically maintains a compressed long-term KV cache alongside the rolling short-term cache. During training rollouts, we compute attention saliency scores across all cached tokens to identify semantically critical frames (scene anchors, motion keyframes, text-aligned moments) and retain compressed representations of these while evicting low-saliency tokens. We train a lightweight saliency predictor jointly with the diffusion model using a temporal consistency auxiliary loss that penalizes semantic drift measured via CLIP embedding distance between frames far apart in the sequence. The compressed long-term cache is updated asynchronously to avoid blocking real-time generation. Experiments: (1) Long-video generation benchmarks (EvalCrafter, VBench) at 5-30 minute equivalent durations; (2) Semantic consistency metrics (CLIP-Sim, temporal LPIPS) vs. fixed rolling window baselines; (3) Ablations on compression ratios, saliency metrics, and update frequencies; (4) Latency-quality trade-offs on single GPU hardware.

title: Contrastive Self Forcing: Improving Long-Horizon Temporal Consistency via Sequence-Level Discriminative Objectives
description: Problem: While Self Forcing addresses exposure bias through autoregressive rollout training, the holistic video-level loss still primarily optimizes pixel-level fidelity. Long-horizon generated videos suffer from semantic drift—gradual inconsistencies in object identity, lighting, and scene coherence—because the training signal doesn't explicitly penalize semantic divergence across distant frames. Proposed Method: We augment Self Forcing with a sequence-level contrastive discriminative objective. During training rollout, we generate multiple candidate video sequences from the same initial context (using different noise seeds) and employ a lightweight temporal consistency discriminator that operates on CLIP-encoded frame embeddings. The discriminator learns to distinguish sequences with coherent long-range semantics from those exhibiting semantic drift by contrasting real video sequences against generated ones and against artificially permuted frame sequences. We combine this contrastive loss with the existing diffusion objective using adaptive loss weighting, and extend the rolling KV cache to maintain a compressed semantic memory of distant frames via learned attention pooling. Experiments: We evaluate on UCF-101, Kinetics-600, and a new long-horizon benchmark (500+ frames) measuring semantic consistency via CLIP cosine similarity across frame pairs at varying temporal distances, FVD, and user studies. We compare against Self Forcing baseline, standard autoregressive diffusion, and ablations removing each component.

title: Adaptive KV Cache Compression for Long-Horizon Autoregressive Video Diffusion via Temporal Saliency Pruning
description:
Problem: Self Forcing enables efficient autoregressive video generation via rolling KV caches, but long-horizon generation (minutes-scale video) remains constrained by memory growth as the KV cache accumulates temporal context. Naively truncating the rolling cache discards potentially critical long-range dependencies (e.g., scene consistency, character appearance), while retaining all keys/values becomes prohibitively expensive.

Proposed Method: We introduce Temporal Saliency Pruning (TSP), a learned cache compression mechanism integrated into the Self Forcing training paradigm. During autoregressive rollout, a lightweight saliency scoring network evaluates each cached frame's KV contribution to current generation quality using attention entropy and gradient-based importance scores. Frames deemed low-saliency are compressed via learned token merging (merging spatially similar tokens within a frame) or fully evicted, maintaining a fixed-size compressed long-term memory alongside a recent full-resolution short-term cache. TSP is trained end-to-end within Self Forcing's holistic video-level loss, allowing the model to learn which temporal context truly matters for coherent long-range generation.

Experiments: (1) Compare TSP against fixed rolling window and full-cache baselines on long-form video generation benchmarks (>500 frames) measuring FVD, CLIP consistency, and GPU memory; (2) Ablate short-term vs. long-term cache size tradeoffs; (3) Evaluate scene consistency on videos with recurring characters/objects; (4) Measure real-time streaming latency at varying compression ratios on a single GPU.

title: Adaptive KV Cache Compression for Long-Horizon Autoregressive Video Diffusion via Temporal Saliency
description: Problem: Self Forcing's rolling KV cache mechanism discards context uniformly based on a fixed window size, ignoring that different past frames carry varying amounts of temporal information. For long-horizon video generation (e.g., minutes-long sequences), this leads to either excessive memory usage or loss of critical context that causes temporal incoherence and semantic drift. Proposed Method: We introduce Temporal Saliency-Guided Cache Compression (TSCC), a learned mechanism that dynamically selects which KV cache entries to retain, compress, or evict based on estimated temporal importance. Specifically, we train a lightweight saliency predictor that attends over cached keys to assign retention scores, then applies learned token merging (inspired by ToMe) to compress low-salience entries while preserving high-salience ones. The saliency predictor is trained end-to-end within the Self Forcing framework using a contrastive temporal consistency loss that penalizes semantic drift when important frames are evicted. Planned Experiments: (1) Long-horizon generation benchmarks (>5 min at 24fps) measuring temporal consistency (CLIP similarity over windows), semantic coherence, and memory footprint; (2) Ablations comparing uniform rolling cache vs. TSCC under matched memory budgets; (3) User studies evaluating perceived narrative coherence; (4) Analysis of which scene types (static vs. dynamic) receive differential compression rates.

title: Scheduled Self Forcing: Curriculum-Based Exposure Blending for Robust Long-Horizon Video Generation
description:
Problem: Self Forcing commits fully to self-generated context during training, which can be destabilizing early in training when the model produces highly noisy outputs, leading to compounding errors that slow convergence and degrade long-horizon coherence. Conversely, ground-truth forcing prevents the model from learning error recovery. A principled middle ground is needed.

Proposed Method: We introduce Scheduled Self Forcing (SSF), a curriculum training strategy that interpolates between ground-truth context and self-generated context using a mixing schedule parameterized by both training progress and temporal distance. Concretely, at each training step, each KV cache slot is stochastically replaced with either a ground-truth frame embedding or a self-generated one according to a beta-distributed mixture coefficient that anneals from ground-truth-dominated to self-generated-dominated over training. We additionally condition on an explicit 'forcing ratio' token, enabling test-time control over how aggressively the model relies on its own outputs—useful for trading off diversity versus coherence during inference. The holistic video-level loss from Self Forcing is retained and augmented with a consistency regularizer penalizing divergence between ground-truth-forced and self-forced predictions.

Experiments: (1) Long-horizon generation benchmarks (256+ frames) measuring FVD and temporal consistency versus vanilla Self Forcing. (2) Ablation of annealing schedules and mixture distributions. (3) Robustness to distribution shift via out-of-domain prompt evaluation. (4) Training stability curves comparing gradient variance across curricula.

title: Scheduled Self Forcing: Curriculum-Based Exposure Annealing for Long-Horizon Video Coherence
description: Problem: Self Forcing eliminates exposure bias by always conditioning on self-generated frames during training, but this cold-start approach forces the model to immediately handle compounding errors from its own noisy outputs, potentially destabilizing early training and limiting long-horizon temporal coherence beyond the training window. Proposed Method: We introduce Scheduled Self Forcing, a curriculum training strategy that smoothly interpolates between ground-truth conditioning and fully self-generated conditioning throughout training. Specifically, we define a mixing schedule p(t) that starts near 1.0 (ground-truth frames) and anneals toward 0.0 (fully self-generated), controlled by a cosine or exponential decay tied to training steps. At each autoregressive step, context frames are sampled stochastically from either ground-truth or previously self-generated outputs according to p(t). We additionally introduce a 'coherence regularization' term that penalizes perceptual drift across segment boundaries using a frozen CLIP-based temporal consistency metric. This regularizer encourages the model to maintain semantic consistency over extended horizons without requiring full backpropagation through the entire rollout. Experiments: We evaluate on UCF-101, Kinetics-600, and an open-domain streaming benchmark, measuring FVD, temporal consistency scores, and generation stability over 60+ second extrapolations, comparing against vanilla Self Forcing, FIFO-Diffusion, and teacher-forcing baselines.

title: Adaptive KV Cache Compression for Long-Horizon Autoregressive Video Diffusion via Temporal Saliency Routing
description: Problem: Self Forcing's rolling KV cache enables streaming video generation but faces a fundamental memory-quality tradeoff: retaining more context frames improves temporal coherence but increases memory and latency, while aggressive cache eviction causes semantic drift over long sequences (e.g., 10+ minute videos). A principled method for selectively retaining the most temporally relevant cached states is lacking. Proposed Method: We introduce Temporal Saliency Routing (TSR), a lightweight learned module that scores cached KV states based on their predicted influence on future frame generation. TSR operates by computing cross-attention importance scores between current query states and cached KV pairs, then dynamically evicting low-importance entries while compressing medium-importance ones via learned vector quantization. Unlike static sliding-window approaches, TSR learns which moments (scene boundaries, object introductions, motion keyframes) are worth preserving indefinitely. We integrate TSR into Self Forcing's training loop so that the saliency module is jointly optimized with the video diffusion model under the holistic video-level loss. Experiments: We evaluate on long-form video benchmarks (VBench-Long, custom 5-minute narrative videos), measuring temporal consistency, semantic coherence, memory footprint, and latency versus fixed rolling-window baselines. Ablations compare static versus learned eviction policies and different compression ratios.

title: Adaptive Rollout Horizon Scheduling for Self-Forcing: Curriculum Learning for Autoregressive Video Diffusion
description:
Problem: Self Forcing's training requires full autoregressive rollout from the start, which exposes the model to heavily corrupted self-generated context early in training when the model is weakest, potentially destabilizing learning and slowing convergence. A naive curriculum that always uses ground-truth context (teacher forcing) delays exposure bias correction, while always using self-generated context (Self Forcing) is computationally expensive and initially noisy.

Proposed Method: We introduce Adaptive Rollout Horizon Scheduling (ARHS), a curriculum learning strategy that dynamically controls the number of self-generated conditioning frames used during training. Early in training, we condition on a short horizon of self-generated frames (1-2 frames) mixed with ground-truth frames, gradually increasing the self-generated rollout length as training progresses. We couple this with a quality-aware scheduling signal: using the model's own FVD/LPIPS estimates on validation sequences to automatically determine when to extend the rollout horizon, rather than relying on fixed epoch-based schedules. We additionally investigate whether stochastic horizon sampling (randomly sampling rollout length each iteration) provides implicit curriculum benefits.

Experiments: We train on UCF-101, Kinetics-600, and a driving video dataset (nuScenes), comparing against vanilla Self Forcing and teacher forcing baselines. Metrics include FVD, training convergence speed, and temporal consistency scores. Ablations examine scheduling strategies (linear, adaptive, stochastic) and horizon lengths.

title: Scheduled Self Forcing: Curriculum-Based Exposure Bias Mitigation for Long-Horizon Video Generation
description: Problem: Self Forcing trains video diffusion models exclusively on self-generated context from the start, which can destabilize early training since the model's own outputs are initially very noisy and far from ground truth. This forces a difficult optimization landscape and may limit convergence to high-quality equilibria for very long video sequences (100+ seconds). Proposed Method: We introduce Scheduled Self Forcing, a curriculum training strategy that smoothly interpolates between ground-truth conditioning and self-generated conditioning throughout training. Inspired by scheduled sampling in RNNs, we define a mixing schedule p(t) that starts near 1.0 (ground-truth frames) and anneals toward 0.0 (fully self-generated frames) as training progresses. Crucially, rather than frame-level mixing, we operate at the chunk level with a differentiable soft-blending mechanism in KV cache space, allowing gradients to flow through the interpolation. We further propose an adaptive scheduling rule based on a drift metric that measures distributional shift between self-generated and ground-truth KV caches, automatically pacing curriculum difficulty. Experiments: (1) Long-video generation quality (FVD, CLIP consistency) on UCF-101 and Kinetics at 30s, 60s, 120s horizons; (2) Training stability curves vs. vanilla Self Forcing; (3) Ablation of scheduling functions (linear, cosine, adaptive); (4) Human preference studies on temporal coherence over extended sequences.

title: Hierarchical Self Forcing: Temporal Consistency Through Multi-Scale Autoregressive Rollout in Long Video Generation
description: Problem: While Self Forcing addresses exposure bias at the frame level, long video generation (minutes-scale) still suffers from semantic drift and narrative inconsistency — generated content gradually deviates from intended high-level structure because autoregressive rollout only enforces local temporal coherence through KV caching of recent frames. Method: We propose Hierarchical Self Forcing, which extends the self-forcing paradigm to operate simultaneously at multiple temporal scales. We introduce a dual-level autoregressive process: a fast stream (frame-level, inheriting Self Forcing's KV cache) and a slow stream (scene-level, maintaining a compressed latent summary of previously generated scenes via a learned temporal abstraction module). During training, both streams undergo joint rollout, with the slow stream providing global conditioning to the fast stream. We employ a hierarchical holistic loss that penalizes both local frame quality and long-range semantic consistency measured via CLIP-based trajectory alignment. A stochastic truncation scheme independently handles gradients across both temporal scales for efficiency. Experiments: (1) Long video generation benchmarks (EvalCrafter-Long, custom 60-second splits of OpenVid), measuring temporal consistency via CLIP score drift over time; (2) Ablations isolating contributions of each hierarchy level; (3) User studies comparing narrative coherence against Self Forcing and non-causal baselines; (4) Computational profiling showing maintained near-real-time generation.

title: Adaptive KV Cache Compression for Long-Horizon Autoregressive Video Diffusion via Temporal Saliency Routing
description: Problem: Self Forcing's rolling KV cache enables efficient streaming video generation, but naively storing all past frame keys and values becomes a bottleneck for very long-horizon generation (minutes of video). Critical temporal context is unevenly distributed—some past frames are highly relevant to future generation while others are redundant—yet existing rolling caches treat all frames uniformly via fixed-window eviction. Method: We propose Temporal Saliency Routing (TSR), a learned cache compression mechanism that dynamically selects which past KV entries to retain, compress, or evict based on cross-attention saliency scores computed during the Self Forcing rollout. Specifically, we train a lightweight gating network that observes per-head attention weights across frames and produces a priority score for each cached token block. Low-priority blocks are either evicted or compressed via a learned vector quantization scheme, while high-priority blocks are preserved at full precision. TSR is trained end-to-end within the Self Forcing framework using the same holistic video-level loss. Experiments: We evaluate on UCF-101, Kinetics-600, and a new 10-minute continuous scene benchmark we construct from HowTo100M clips.
