Metrics include FVD, memory footprint vs. generation length scaling curves, latency at 100+ frame horizons, and a human study on temporal coherence. We compare against fixed rolling windows, random eviction, and attention-sink baselines.

title: Curriculum Self Forcing: Adaptive Exposure Scheduling for Long-Horizon Video Generation
description:
Problem: Self Forcing trains autoregressive video diffusion models by always conditioning on self-generated frames, but this abrupt switch from ground-truth to fully self-generated context during training can destabilize early training and cause error accumulation over very long sequences (thousands of frames). A principled curriculum for gradually increasing self-generation exposure remains unexplored.

Proposed Method: We introduce Curriculum Self Forcing, which replaces the binary ground-truth/self-generated context with a differentiable mixture schedule. During training, each context frame is drawn from either the ground-truth distribution or the model's own autoregressive rollout with probability p(t), where p(t) follows a learned curriculum that starts near zero and anneals toward one as training progresses. We parameterize the curriculum with a small meta-network trained via bilevel optimization to minimize validation sequence-level loss, automatically discovering the optimal exposure ramp. Additionally, we introduce a 'context dropout' regularizer that randomly masks KV cache entries, forcing the model to remain robust to imperfect or partial context.

Experiments: (1) Long-horizon generation quality (FVD, LPIPS) on Kinetics-600 and UCF-101 at 512+ frame horizons vs. vanilla Self Forcing. (2) Training stability curves comparing fixed vs. learned curriculum schedules. (3) Ablations on curriculum shape (linear, cosine, learned). (4) Downstream application to autonomous driving video prediction (nuScenes) where long-horizon rollout quality is safety-critical.

title: Adaptive Rollout Depth Scheduling for Self-Forcing: Curriculum Learning for Autoregressive Video Diffusion
description:
Problem: Self Forcing trains autoregressive video diffusion by rolling out entire sequences from scratch, exposing the model to its own errors throughout training. However, early in training when the model generates highly noisy outputs, conditioning on self-generated frames introduces extremely high-variance gradients that destabilize learning. A curriculum that gradually increases the proportion of self-generated context versus ground-truth context could improve training stability and final quality.

Proposed Method: We introduce Adaptive Rollout Depth Scheduling (ARDS), a curriculum learning strategy that dynamically controls the mixture between ground-truth and self-generated KV cache context during training. Early training phases use predominantly ground-truth context (shallow rollout), gradually increasing rollout depth as training progresses. We formalize this as a scheduled interpolation in KV cache space, blending cached ground-truth and self-generated keys/values with a time-varying mixing coefficient governed by training step and current generation quality metrics. We additionally propose a quality-aware rollout gate that uses a lightweight discriminator signal to adaptively determine when self-generated frames are reliable enough to serve as context.

Experiments: We evaluate on UCF-101, WebVid, and an in-house driving dataset, measuring FVD, temporal consistency, and training convergence speed. Ablations compare fixed rollout depth, linear scheduling, and quality-gated scheduling. We analyze gradient variance throughout training and demonstrate improved sample quality with fewer training steps compared to vanilla Self Forcing.

title: Adversarial Self Forcing: Training-Time Discriminator Guidance for Temporal Coherence in Autoregressive Video Diffusion
description: Problem: While Self Forcing addresses exposure bias via autoregressive rollout during training, the holistic video-level loss still operates primarily in pixel/latent reconstruction space, which may inadequately penalize subtle temporal inconsistencies (flickering, identity drift, physics violations) that are perceptually salient but reconstruction-loss-invisible. Proposed Method: We augment Self Forcing's training paradigm with a lightweight temporal discriminator that operates over the KV-cache-generated video sequences during training rollouts. The discriminator receives sliding windows of self-generated frames and learns to distinguish them from real video clips, providing adversarial gradient signal complementary to the diffusion denoising loss. To avoid mode collapse and training instability common in video GANs, we use a frozen pretrained video encoder (e.g., VideoMAE) as discriminator backbone with only a thin classification head trained, and apply spectral normalization. The discriminator loss is integrated with stochastic gradient truncation from Self Forcing, ensuring backpropagation only through a bounded number of autoregressive steps. Experiments: (1) Compare temporal consistency metrics (CLIP-T, flow warping error, FVD) against baseline Self Forcing on UCF-101, Kinetics, and WebVid; (2) Ablate discriminator architecture choices and window sizes; (3) Evaluate long-horizon extrapolation (100+ frames) for drift accumulation; (4) Measure training wall-clock overhead versus quality gains.

title: Scheduled Self Forcing: Curriculum-Based Exposure Annealing for Long-Horizon Video Coherence
description:
Problem: Self Forcing eliminates exposure bias by conditioning entirely on self-generated frames during training, but abruptly switching from ground-truth to self-generated context can destabilize early training and hurt long-range semantic coherence in very long videos (hundreds of frames). A curriculum that gradually transitions from ground-truth to self-generated conditioning could yield more stable optimization and better long-range consistency.

Proposed Method: We introduce Scheduled Self Forcing, which interpolates between teacher-forced (ground-truth context) and self-forced (model-generated context) training using a mixing schedule that anneals the ground-truth fraction from 1.0 to 0 over training. At each training step, context frames are stochastically drawn from either ground-truth or previously self-generated outputs according to the current schedule. We additionally propose a semantic anchoring loss that penalizes drift in CLIP-space embeddings across distant frames, discouraging topic and style drift in long sequences. The rolling KV cache from Self Forcing is retained but augmented with a learned gating mechanism that selectively attenuates stale context.

Experiments: (1) Compare coherence metrics (CLIP consistency, FVD, LPIPS drift) on UCF-101, WebVid, and a new 5-minute video benchmark at 100+ frame horizons. (2) Ablate annealing schedules (linear, cosine, step). (3) Measure training stability via gradient variance curves. (4) Human evaluation of long-video semantic coherence vs. vanilla Self Forcing.
